283	**[2.4 Scope and Role of Operable Units]{.underline}**
284	
285	EPA has designated four operable units for the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site to organize and manage the remedial action in a logical manner that addresses the full spatial extent and media-specific nature of contamination at the Site. This ROD addresses all four operable units in a single comprehensive remedial action decision. The four operable units are described below.
286	
287	**Operable Unit 1 (OU-1): Former Production Area.** OU-1 encompasses approximately 18 acres of the central portion of the Site, corresponding to the footprint of the former manufacturing buildings, drum storage areas, tank farms, and surrounding soils. OU-1 addresses the most heavily contaminated soils at the Site, including the DNAPL source zone, which is the primary ongoing source of dissolved-phase groundwater contamination. The primary contaminants in OU-1 soils include TCE, PCE, pentachlorophenol, hexavalent chromium, and benzo(a)pyrene.
288	
289	**Operable Unit 2 (OU-2): Wastewater Lagoon Area.** OU-2 encompasses approximately 8 acres in the southwestern portion of the Site, including the locations of three former unlined wastewater lagoons and the surrounding buffer areas. The lagoons contain contaminated sediments and sludges, and the underlying soils are contaminated to the depth of the native clay confining layer. The primary contaminants in OU-2 include VOCs, semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs), and metals.
290	
291	**Operable Unit 3 (OU-3): Groundwater Plume.** OU-3 encompasses the dissolved-phase groundwater contamination plume that extends from beneath OU-1 and OU-2 in a southeasterly direction toward Millhaven Creek and the Ashford County public water supply wellfield. The plume is approximately 1.2 miles long and 0.4 miles wide, as delineated during the Remedial Investigation. The primary groundwater contaminants include TCE, PCE, 1,4-dioxane, and hexavalent chromium.
292	
293	**Operable Unit 4 (OU-4): Riparian Corridor.** OU-4 encompasses approximately 4.5 acres of contaminated floodplain soils along Millhaven Creek, south of the main facility area. Contamination in OU-4 resulted from historical surface water runoff and overbank flooding that transported contaminated materials from the facility to the riparian corridor.
294	
295	**[2.5 Site Characteristics]{.underline}**
296	
297	**2.5.1 Physical Setting and Geology**
298	
299	The Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site is situated in the glaciated portion of western Ohio, within the Eastern Corn Belt Plains ecoregion. The regional topography is gently rolling, with elevations in the Millhaven area ranging from approximately 920 to 980 feet above mean sea level (amsl). The Site itself is relatively flat, with elevations ranging from approximately 935 feet amsl at the northern property boundary to approximately 925 feet amsl along Millhaven Creek at the southern property boundary, resulting in a gentle southward slope.
300	
301	The climate in Ashford County is humid continental, with average annual precipitation of approximately 39 inches. Average temperatures range from approximately 26°F in January to 75°F in July. The frost depth for design purposes in western Ohio is approximately 32 inches.
302	
303	The regional geology at the Site is characteristic of the glaciated Till Plains of western Ohio. Surface soils at the Site consist of fill materials and disturbed native soils overlying glacial deposits. The glacial stratigraphy, as characterized during the Remedial Investigation through the installation and logging of more than 120 soil borings and monitoring wells, generally consists of the following sequence from the surface downward:
304	
305	> • **Fill and disturbed soils (0 to approximately 3 feet bgs):** Mixed fill materials including gravel, demolition debris, and reworked native soils.
306	>
307	> • **Glacial outwash sand and gravel (approximately 3 to 15 feet bgs in the OU-1 area; 3 to 12 feet bgs in the OU-2 area):** Medium to coarse sand with varying proportions of gravel, representing the shallow aquifer zone. This unit is the primary zone of soil contamination and the principal water-bearing unit for the shallow groundwater system.
308	>
309	> • **Native glacial clay (lacustrine clay till) (approximately 12 to 15 feet bgs in the lagoon area; 15 to 30 feet bgs in the production area):** Dense, low-permeability clay serving as an aquitard separating the shallow aquifer from the deeper bedrock aquifer. This clay layer is continuous across the Site based on RI borings and serves as the natural confining unit.
310	>
311	> • **Bedrock (Silurian-age dolomite and limestone):** Encountered at depths ranging from approximately 30 to 50 feet bgs. The bedrock aquifer is a regional water supply aquifer and is the source aquifer for the Ashford County public water supply wellfield.
312	
313	Groundwater in the shallow aquifer flows generally to the southeast, toward Millhaven Creek, with a hydraulic gradient of approximately 0.008 feet per foot (ft/ft). Hydraulic conductivity of the glacial outwash sand and gravel was determined from slug tests and pumping tests during the RI to range from approximately 15 to 45 feet per day (ft/day), with a geometric mean of approximately 28 ft/day. The shallow aquifer is unconfined to semi-confined, with a saturated thickness of approximately 8 to 12 feet across most of the Site. Groundwater recharge occurs primarily through infiltration of precipitation through the permeable surficial soils.
314	
315	Millhaven Creek receives groundwater discharge from the shallow aquifer along its reach adjacent to and downstream of the Site. Surface water sampling during the RI confirmed that contaminated groundwater is discharging to Millhaven Creek, contributing dissolved-phase contaminants to the stream.
316	
317	**2.5.2 Nature and Extent of Contamination**
318	
319	The Remedial Investigation, completed in 2019, comprehensively characterized the nature and extent of contamination at the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site through the collection and analysis of more than 2,800 environmental samples, including soil, groundwater, surface water, sediment, and soil vapor samples. The principal contaminants of concern (COCs) and the maximum detected concentrations in affected media are summarized below, along with the applicable standards or screening levels used to evaluate the significance of contamination.
320	
321	**Groundwater Contaminants of Concern:**
322	
323	> • **Trichloroethylene (TCE):** Maximum detected concentration of 4,800 µg/L in the shallow aquifer directly beneath the OU-1 DNAPL source zone. The federal Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for TCE is 5 µg/L. TCE concentrations exceed the MCL in an area extending approximately 1.2 miles downgradient of the source area.
324	>
325	> • **Tetrachloroethylene (PCE):** Maximum detected concentration of 1,250 µg/L in the shallow aquifer beneath OU-1. The federal MCL for PCE is 5 µg/L. PCE is co-located with the TCE plume and exhibits a similar distribution pattern, though at generally lower concentrations.
326	>
327	> • **1,4-Dioxane:** Maximum detected concentration of 320 µg/L in the shallow aquifer downgradient of OU-1 and OU-2. The EPA Health Advisory Level for 1,4-dioxane is 0.35 µg/L. 1,4-Dioxane was historically used as a stabilizer in chlorinated solvent formulations manufactured at the facility. Due to its high water solubility (miscible with water) and low retardation in the subsurface, 1,4-dioxane has migrated farther downgradient than the chlorinated solvent plume and represents the leading edge of the contaminant plume approaching the Ashford County public water supply wellfield.
328	>
329	> • **Hexavalent Chromium:** Maximum detected concentration of 285 µg/L in the shallow aquifer beneath the former chrome plating area within OU-1. The federal MCL for total chromium is 100 µg/L.
330	
331	**Soil Contaminants of Concern:**
332	
333	> • **Pentachlorophenol (PCP):** Maximum detected concentration of 3,200 mg/kg in surface and subsurface soils in the former wood treatment area within OU-1. The EPA residential preliminary remediation goal (PRG) for PCP is 0.3 mg/kg; the industrial PRG is 3.8 mg/kg.
334	>
335	> • **Hexavalent Chromium:** Maximum detected concentration of 890 mg/kg in soils beneath the former chrome plating building in OU-1. The industrial PRG for hexavalent chromium is 6.3 mg/kg.
336	>
337	> • **Benzo(a)pyrene:** Maximum detected concentration of 45 mg/kg in soils in the former tank farm area within OU-1. The industrial PRG for benzo(a)pyrene is 2.1 mg/kg.
338	
339	**Contamination Distribution by Operable Unit:**
340	
341	In **OU-1**, soil contamination extends from the surface to approximately 15 feet bgs in the most heavily impacted areas, corresponding to the depth of the glacial outwash sand and gravel unit overlying the native clay layer. The most significant contamination is concentrated in the former production building footprints, drum storage areas, and the tank farm. DNAPL (primarily TCE) has been identified in the subsurface beneath OU-1 at depths ranging from approximately 10 to 25 feet bgs, extending into and pooling upon the upper surface of the native clay confining layer.
342	
343	In **OU-2**, contaminated sediments within the three former unlined wastewater lagoons extend from the surface to the native clay layer at approximately 12 feet bgs. The lagoon sediments contain elevated concentrations of VOCs, SVOCs, pesticides, and metals, reflecting decades of uncontrolled wastewater disposal.
344	
345	In **OU-3**, the dissolved-phase groundwater plume extends approximately 1.2 miles in a southeasterly direction from the source areas beneath OU-1 and OU-2. Contaminant concentrations generally decrease with increasing distance from the source areas, though TCE concentrations still exceed the MCL at the leading edge of the plume. The 1,4-dioxane plume extends beyond the chlorinated solvent plume due to its greater mobility in groundwater.
346	
347	In **OU-4**, contaminated floodplain soils along Millhaven Creek are impacted to a depth of approximately 3 feet bgs. Contamination in the riparian corridor is attributable to historical surface water runoff and overbank flooding events that deposited contaminated sediments across the floodplain.
348	
349	**2.5.3 DNAPL Source Characterization**
350	
351	The DNAPL source zone at OU-1 represents the most significant ongoing source of dissolved-phase groundwater contamination at the Site. DNAPL characterization activities conducted during the RI included the installation of multi-level monitoring wells, membrane interface probe (MIP) profiling, and direct-push soil sampling across the former production area. DNAPL was positively identified in 8 soil borings distributed across a 3.5-acre area within OU-1, concentrated beneath the former manufacturing buildings and the drum storage yard.
352	
353	The vertical extent of DNAPL ranges from approximately 10 to 25 feet bgs, with the greatest accumulations occurring at and just above the interface between the glacial outwash sand and gravel and the underlying native clay confining layer. DNAPL composition analysis indicates that the non-aqueous phase consists primarily of trichloroethylene (TCE), with lesser amounts of tetrachloroethylene (PCE) and other chlorinated organic compounds. Estimated DNAPL saturation within the source zone ranges from approximately 5 to 18 percent of pore volume based on partitioning interwell tracer test (PITT) results.
354	
355	The DNAPL source zone is the primary ongoing source feeding the dissolved-phase groundwater plume (OU-3). Mass flux calculations performed during the FS estimated that the DNAPL source zone releases approximately 12 to 18 kilograms per year of dissolved TCE to the groundwater. Effective DNAPL recovery and source mass reduction are essential to achieving long-term groundwater cleanup objectives within the 30-year remedial action timeframe established in this ROD. Without aggressive source reduction, groundwater modeling indicates that the dissolved-phase plume would continue to expand and could reach the Ashford County public water supply wellfield within approximately 15 to 20 years under current conditions.
356	
357	**[2.6 Current and Potential Future Land and Resource Uses]{.underline}**
358	
359	The Hargrove Industrial Complex property is currently classified as a vacant industrial property. No active industrial, commercial, or residential activities are conducted at the Site. The property is secured with chain-link fencing and is posted with \"No Trespassing\" signs. The property is zoned for industrial use under the Ashford County zoning ordinance.
360	
361	Future land use at the Site shall be restricted to industrial and commercial purposes through the implementation of institutional controls, specifically an environmental covenant to be recorded with the Ashford County Recorder\'s Office pursuant to Ohio Revised Code Chapter 5301.80 et seq. (Uniform Environmental Covenants Act). The institutional controls shall prohibit residential development, restrict excavation activities without prior EPA approval, and prohibit the installation of groundwater extraction wells for drinking water purposes on the Site property.
362	
363	Groundwater beneath and downgradient of the Site is not currently used as a source of drinking water due to the presence of contamination. However, the Ashford County public water supply wellfield, located 1.8 miles downgradient of the leading edge of the groundwater plume, is a current and significant beneficial use of the regional bedrock aquifer. This wellfield serves approximately 14,000 residents and represents a resource that must be protected from contamination. Millhaven Creek is a perennial stream classified by the Ohio EPA as a warm water habitat stream supporting aquatic life communities and used for recreational fishing by area residents.
364	
365	**[2.7 Summary of Site Risks]{.underline}**
366	
367	**2.7.1 Human Health Risk Assessment**
368	
369	A baseline human health risk assessment (BHHRA) was conducted as part of the Remedial Investigation to evaluate the potential risks to human health from exposure to contaminants at the Site under current and reasonably anticipated future conditions. The BHHRA was conducted in accordance with EPA\'s Risk Assessment Guidance for Superfund (RAGS) and evaluated risks associated with the following exposure scenarios: industrial worker (current and future land use), construction/utility worker, and hypothetical resident (to evaluate the need for institutional controls). The risk assessment evaluated exposure via multiple pathways, including direct contact with contaminated soils, incidental ingestion of contaminated soils, inhalation of fugitive dust and volatile emissions, ingestion of contaminated groundwater, and vapor intrusion into occupied structures.
370	
371	The BHHRA identified unacceptable risks across multiple exposure scenarios and pathways. The key findings are summarized below.
372	
373	**Cancer Risks.** The cumulative excess lifetime cancer risk (ELCR) for the reasonable maximum exposure (RME) industrial worker scenario was calculated at approximately 3 × 10⁻³ (3 in 1,000), which exceeds EPA\'s target cancer risk range of 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴. The primary cancer risk drivers were identified as: TCE in groundwater via ingestion and vapor intrusion pathways; PCE in groundwater via ingestion and vapor intrusion; pentachlorophenol in soil via direct contact and incidental ingestion; benzo(a)pyrene in soil via direct contact and incidental ingestion; and hexavalent chromium in soil via inhalation of particulates. For the hypothetical future residential scenario, the cumulative ELCR was approximately 2 × 10⁻², confirming the need for institutional controls to prevent residential development.
374	
375	**Non-Cancer Hazards.** The non-cancer hazard index (HI) for the groundwater ingestion pathway was calculated at 47, which significantly exceeds the acceptable threshold of 1.0. The primary non-cancer hazard drivers included TCE (liver and kidney effects), PCE (liver effects), hexavalent chromium (gastrointestinal and hepatic effects), and 1,4-dioxane (liver and kidney effects). The HI for the soil direct contact/incidental ingestion pathway for the industrial worker scenario was 8.2, also exceeding the acceptable threshold.
376	
377	**Vapor Intrusion.** The vapor intrusion pathway was evaluated using both Johnson-Ettinger model predictions and sub-slab soil vapor sampling data. Results indicated that vapor intrusion of TCE into hypothetical future occupied structures in the OU-1 area would pose unacceptable cancer risks and non-cancer hazards, further supporting the need for source removal and groundwater remediation.
378	
379	**Threat to Public Water Supply.** Groundwater transport modeling conducted during the FS indicated that the dissolved-phase contaminant plume, if uncontrolled, could reach the Ashford County public water supply wellfield within approximately 15 to 20 years, potentially exposing approximately 14,000 residents to contaminated drinking water. This potential exposure pathway was identified as the most significant human health threat associated with the Site.
380	
381	**2.7.2 Ecological Risk Assessment**
382	
383	A screening-level ecological risk assessment (SLERA) and a baseline ecological risk assessment (BERA) were conducted as part of the Remedial Investigation to evaluate potential risks to ecological receptors from Site-related contamination. The ecological risk assessments focused on aquatic and riparian receptors in and adjacent to Millhaven Creek (OU-4 and adjacent surface water), which represent the primary ecological exposure pathways at the Site.
384	
385	The SLERA identified multiple contaminants in surface water, sediment, and floodplain soils at concentrations exceeding ecological screening benchmarks, including ambient water quality criteria for aquatic life protection and sediment quality guidelines. Based on the SLERA results, a BERA was conducted to quantify risks to specific ecological receptor groups.
386	
387	The BERA evaluated risks to the following representative ecological receptors: benthic macroinvertebrate communities, fish (fathead minnow and bluegill sunfish), piscivorous birds (belted kingfisher), and riparian mammals (mink and short-tailed shrew). The BERA identified ecological hazard quotients exceeding 1.0 for multiple contaminant-receptor-pathway combinations, indicating potential adverse effects on aquatic and riparian communities.
388	
389	Benthic macroinvertebrate community surveys conducted during the RI documented significantly impaired diversity and abundance in Millhaven Creek downstream of the Site compared to upstream reference stations. The downstream communities exhibited reduced taxa richness, reduced Ephemeroptera-Plecoptera-Trichoptera (EPT) index values, and dominance by pollution-tolerant species, consistent with impacts from contaminated groundwater discharge and contaminated floodplain runoff.
390	
391	Ecological risk-based screening levels were developed for floodplain soil COCs to define the extent of ecological contamination requiring remediation in OU-4. These screening levels were derived using site-specific ecological exposure parameters and toxicity reference values from the EPA Ecological Soil Screening Levels (Eco-SSLs) and other peer-reviewed sources.
392	
393	**2.7.3 Basis for Response Action**
394	
395	The response action selected in this ROD is necessary to protect human health and the environment from actual and threatened releases of hazardous substances from the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site. The presence of hazardous substances in soil and groundwater at concentrations significantly exceeding federal and state standards and risk-based criteria, combined with the documented threat to the Ashford County public water supply wellfield, the impairment of Millhaven Creek ecological communities, and the potential for human exposure through multiple pathways, warrants implementation of the comprehensive remedial action described in this ROD. The unacceptable risks identified in the baseline risk assessments cannot be adequately addressed through monitoring or institutional controls alone.
396	
397	**[2.8 Remedial Action Objectives]{.underline}**
398	
399	Remedial action objectives (RAOs) have been established for each operable unit to define the goals that the Selected Remedy must achieve to protect human health and the environment. The RAOs were developed based on the results of the baseline risk assessments, the identified contaminants of concern and their concentrations, applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements, and current and reasonably anticipated future land and resource uses.
400	
401	**OU-1 Remedial Action Objectives:**
402	
403	1\. Prevent direct contact with, incidental ingestion of, and inhalation of contaminated soils at concentrations exceeding industrial preliminary remediation goals.
404	
405	2\. Remove or treat DNAPL source mass to reduce the ongoing contribution of dissolved-phase contaminants to groundwater to the maximum extent practicable, thereby supporting achievement of groundwater cleanup objectives within the remedial action timeframe.
406	
407	3\. Achieve soil cleanup levels (industrial PRGs) within 5 years of construction completion.
408	
409	**OU-2 Remedial Action Objectives:**
410	
411	1\. Prevent migration of contaminants from lagoon sediments and underlying contaminated soils to groundwater.
412	
413	2\. Contain lagoon materials in a manner protective of groundwater quality and that prevents direct human and ecological exposure to contaminated materials.
414	
415	**OU-3 Remedial Action Objectives:**
416	
417	1\. Restore groundwater to beneficial use by achieving cleanup levels at point of compliance wells within 30 years of initial system startup.
418	
419	2\. Prevent further migration of the dissolved-phase contaminant plume toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield.
420	
421	3\. Achieve the following groundwater cleanup levels at point of compliance wells located at the Site boundary:
422	
423	> • Trichloroethylene (TCE): ≤ 5 µg/L (federal MCL)
424	>
425	> • Tetrachloroethylene (PCE): ≤ 5 µg/L (federal MCL)
426	>
427	> • 1,4-Dioxane: ≤ 0.35 µg/L (EPA Health Advisory Level)
428	>
429	> • Hexavalent Chromium: ≤ 100 µg/L (federal MCL for total chromium)
430	
431	**OU-4 Remedial Action Objectives:**
432	
433	1\. Prevent ecological exposure to contaminated floodplain soils at concentrations exceeding ecological risk-based screening levels.
434	
435	2\. Restore the riparian corridor along Millhaven Creek to support native ecological communities, including benthic macroinvertebrate populations, fish communities, and riparian vegetation.
436	
437	**Overall Performance Standards and Timeframes.** The Selected Remedy shall achieve remedial action objectives within 30 years for groundwater cleanup (OU-3) and within 5 years for soil and source area cleanup (OU-1, OU-2, and OU-4), measured from the commencement of active remediation. These timeframes are based on remedial alternative modeling conducted during the Feasibility Study and represent the estimated period required to achieve the stated RAOs under the Selected Remedy, subject to adjustment during five-year reviews based on actual remedy performance data.
438	
439	**[2.9 Description of Alternatives]{.underline}**
440	
441	The Feasibility Study evaluated a range of remedial alternatives for each operable unit, consistent with EPA guidance (OSWER Directive 9355.3-01FS) and the NCP, 40 CFR § 300.430(e). The alternatives were developed to span the range of possible remedial approaches, from no action to the most aggressive treatment options, and were screened against effectiveness, implementability, and cost criteria. The alternatives retained for detailed analysis for each operable unit are described below.
442	
443	**2.9.1 OU-1 Alternatives**
444	
445	**Alternative 1: No Action.** Under the No Action alternative, no remedial activities would be conducted at OU-1. This alternative serves as a baseline for comparison with the other alternatives, as required by the NCP. The No Action alternative would not address contaminated soils, the DNAPL source zone, or direct contact risks. No institutional controls or monitoring would be implemented. Estimated present-value cost: \$0.
446	
447	**Alternative 2: Institutional Controls and Monitoring Only.** This alternative would implement institutional controls to restrict land use to industrial/commercial purposes and would establish a long-term groundwater and soil monitoring program. No active soil treatment, excavation, or DNAPL recovery would be conducted. While this alternative would reduce the potential for direct human exposure through land use restrictions, it would not address the DNAPL source zone or reduce the ongoing contribution of dissolved contaminants to groundwater. Estimated present-value cost: \$2.1 million.
448

record-of-decision.part.01:115:**Alternative 3: Excavation, Thermal Desorption, and DNAPL Recovery (Selected Remedy).** This alternative combines excavation of contaminated soils to 15 feet bgs (42,000 cubic yards), DNAPL recovery via steam-enhanced extraction using 14 injection/extraction well pairs, and ex-situ thermal desorption of excavated soils to a treatment standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs. Treated soils meeting the standard may be used as on-site backfill; soils not meeting the standard are disposed off-site at a RCRA Subtitle C facility. Institutional controls would restrict future land use. This alternative provides aggressive source removal and treatment, significantly reduces the ongoing contaminant mass flux to groundwater, and utilizes treatment technologies to reduce the toxicity, mobility, and volume of contaminants. Estimated present-value cost: \$31.2 million.

**Alternative 3: Excavation, Thermal Desorption, and DNAPL Recovery (Selected Remedy).** This alternative combines excavation of contaminated soils to 15 feet bgs (42,000 cubic yards), DNAPL recovery via steam-enhanced extraction using 14 injection/extraction well pairs, and ex-situ thermal desorption of excavated soils to a treatment standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs. Treated soils meeting the standard may be used as on-site backfill; soils not meeting the standard are disposed off-site at a RCRA Subtitle C facility. Institutional controls would restrict future land use. This alternative provides aggressive source removal and treatment, significantly reduces the ongoing contaminant mass flux to groundwater, and utilizes treatment technologies to reduce the toxicity, mobility, and volume of contaminants. Estimated present-value cost: \$31.2 million.

**Alternative 4: In-Situ Chemical Oxidation (ISCO) and Capping.** This alternative would implement in-situ chemical oxidation using potassium permanganate or sodium persulfate to treat contaminated soils and DNAPL in place, followed by installation of an engineered cap to prevent direct contact and infiltration. While ISCO can reduce contaminant mass in the source zone, its effectiveness for DNAPL remediation is limited by the difficulty of achieving adequate contact between the oxidant and DNAPL in heterogeneous subsurface materials. Capping would limit direct contact exposure but would not achieve permanent source removal. Estimated present-value cost: \$22.8 million.

**Alternative 5: Full Excavation and Off-Site Disposal.** This alternative would excavate all contaminated soils to the full depth and lateral extent of contamination and transport the excavated materials to a permitted RCRA Subtitle C disposal facility. This alternative would achieve the most complete source removal but at substantially higher cost due to the large volume of materials requiring off-site disposal and the associated transportation costs. Estimated present-value cost: \$48.5 million.

**2.9.2 OU-2 Alternatives**

**Alternative 1: No Action.** No remedial activities would be conducted at OU-2. Contaminated lagoon sediments and underlying soils would remain in place. This alternative does not address the ongoing release of contaminants from the lagoon area to groundwater. Estimated present-value cost: \$0.

**Alternative 2: Capping in Place with Monitoring.** This alternative would install an engineered cap over the three former lagoon areas to prevent infiltration and direct contact. Long-term monitoring would track groundwater quality downgradient of the lagoons. While capping would reduce infiltration-driven contaminant migration, it would not remove contaminated materials from their current location in direct contact with the shallow aquifer. Estimated present-value cost: \$8.4 million.

**Alternative 3: Excavation and On-Site Containment (Selected Remedy).** This alternative involves excavation of lagoon sediments and contaminated soils to the native clay layer (approximately 12 feet bgs), consolidation in an on-site engineered containment cell with a composite liner (60-mil HDPE over 2-foot compacted clay) and RCRA-equivalent cap, leachate collection and treatment at the on-site groundwater treatment plant, and long-term monitoring with a minimum of 8 downgradient wells. This alternative removes contaminated materials from direct contact with the aquifer and consolidates them in a protective containment system while avoiding the significantly higher cost of off-site disposal. Estimated present-value cost: \$18.7 million.

**Alternative 4: Full Excavation and Off-Site Disposal.** All lagoon sediments and contaminated soils would be excavated, stabilized as necessary, and transported to a permitted RCRA Subtitle C facility for disposal. This alternative provides the most permanent solution for OU-2 materials but at substantially higher cost. Estimated present-value cost: \$34.2 million.

**2.9.3 OU-3 Alternatives**

**Alternative 1: No Action.** No remedial activities would be conducted to address the groundwater plume. The plume would continue to migrate toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield. Estimated present-value cost: \$0.

**Alternative 2: Monitored Natural Attenuation (MNA).** This alternative would rely on natural processes, including dilution, dispersion, sorption, and biodegradation, to reduce contaminant concentrations over time. A comprehensive monitoring network would be established to verify attenuation rates and detect any acceleration of plume migration. While natural attenuation processes are occurring at the Site, the FS determined that MNA alone would require in excess of 100 years to achieve groundwater cleanup levels for TCE and PCE, and would not effectively attenuate 1,4-dioxane, which is resistant to natural biodegradation under the aerobic to moderately reducing conditions present at the Site. MNA alone was rejected as insufficiently protective given the proximity of the public water supply wellfield. Estimated present-value cost: \$4.8 million.

**Alternative 3: Pump-and-Treat Only.** This alternative would install an extraction well system to capture and contain the plume, with above-ground treatment using air stripping and GAC. This alternative would provide plume containment but would not include AOP treatment or in-situ bioremediation. Without AOP treatment, the pump-and-treat system could not achieve the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level of 0.35 µg/L, because 1,4-dioxane is resistant to conventional adsorption on granular activated carbon due to its high water solubility (miscible with water) and low octanol-water partition coefficient (log Kow = −0.27). The low Henry\'s Law constant of 1,4-dioxane (4.80 × 10⁻⁶ atm·m³/mol) also renders conventional air stripping ineffective for this compound. Without in-situ ERD, the timeframe to achieve cleanup levels for chlorinated solvents would be significantly extended beyond 30 years. Estimated present-value cost: \$21.3 million.

**Alternative 4: Pump-and-Treat with In-Situ ERD and AOP Treatment (Selected Remedy).** This alternative combines pump-and-treat with 12 extraction wells along a 2,400-foot extraction trench, an on-site treatment train (air stripping, GAC, and AOP using UV/hydrogen peroxide for 1,4-dioxane), NPDES discharge to Millhaven Creek, in-situ ERD with 48 injection points at 30-foot centers, and a comprehensive monitoring network. The AOP unit is specifically included to address 1,4-dioxane, which is not effectively treated by air stripping or GAC alone. The ERD component accelerates biodegradation of chlorinated solvents in the mid-plume area, reducing the timeframe to achieve cleanup levels. This alternative represents the most effective combination of active and passive treatment technologies to achieve groundwater RAOs within 30 years. Estimated present-value cost: \$28.9 million.

**Alternative 5: In-Situ Thermal Treatment of Full Plume.** This alternative would apply in-situ thermal treatment (electrical resistance heating or thermal conductive heating) across the full extent of the 1.2-mile plume to volatilize dissolved-phase contaminants for recovery and above-ground treatment. While technically aggressive, this approach would be extremely energy-intensive, difficult to implement across the full plume extent (including areas beneath Millhaven Creek), and prohibitively expensive. The technology is also not effective for 1,4-dioxane at the dissolved-phase concentrations present in the distal portions of the plume. Estimated present-value cost: \$112.6 million.

**2.9.4 OU-4 Alternatives**

**Alternative 1: No Action.** No remedial activities would be conducted in the riparian corridor. Contaminated floodplain soils would remain in place, and ecological exposure would continue. Estimated present-value cost: \$0.

**Alternative 2: Institutional Controls and Monitoring.** This alternative would implement institutional controls to restrict access to the riparian corridor and establish a long-term ecological monitoring program. No physical remediation would be conducted. While access restrictions would limit some human exposure, ecological receptors would continue to be exposed to contaminated soils. This alternative would not restore the riparian corridor to support native ecological communities. Estimated present-value cost: \$1.9 million.

**Alternative 3: Excavation and Ecological Restoration (Selected Remedy).** This alternative involves excavation of contaminated floodplain soils to 3 feet bgs (6,800 cubic yards), restoration with clean fill, topsoil, and native riparian vegetation per a Habitat Restoration Plan approved by USFWS and ODNR, and a 5-year ecological monitoring program. This alternative provides permanent removal of contaminated materials, restores the riparian corridor to support native ecological communities, and includes monitoring to verify restoration success. Estimated present-value cost: \$10.6 million.

**[2.10 Comparative Analysis of Alternatives]{.underline}**

The remedial alternatives for each operable unit were evaluated against the nine criteria specified in the NCP, 40 CFR § 300.430(e)(9)(iii). The first two criteria (overall protection of human health and the environment, and compliance with ARARs) are \"threshold\" criteria that must be satisfied for an alternative to be eligible for selection. The next five criteria (long-term effectiveness and permanence; reduction of toxicity, mobility, or volume through treatment; short-term effectiveness; implementability; and cost) are \"balancing\" criteria used to weigh the relative merits of alternatives. The final two criteria (state acceptance and community acceptance) are \"modifying\" criteria evaluated based on stakeholder input.

**Threshold Criteria:**

*1. Overall Protection of Human Health and the Environment.* The No Action alternatives for all four OUs fail this criterion. Among the active alternatives, the Selected Remedy alternatives for each OU provide the highest degree of overall protectiveness when balanced against implementability and cost. For OU-1, Alternative 3 provides superior protectiveness compared to Alternative 4 (ISCO/capping) because it achieves permanent source removal rather than in-situ treatment with uncertain effectiveness. For OU-3, Alternative 4 is more protective than Alternative 3 (pump-and-treat only) because it includes AOP treatment necessary to achieve the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level and ERD to accelerate plume remediation.

*2. Compliance with ARARs.* The Selected Remedy alternatives for all four OUs comply with, or provide a basis for invoking waivers of, all applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements. The No Action alternatives and monitoring-only alternatives do not achieve chemical-specific ARARs within a reasonable timeframe.

**Balancing Criteria:**

*3. Long-Term Effectiveness and Permanence.* The Selected Remedy alternatives provide high long-term effectiveness. OU-1 Alternative 3 permanently removes contaminated soils and DNAPL mass. OU-2 Alternative 3 provides effective long-term containment with monitoring. OU-3 Alternative 4 is projected to achieve cleanup levels within 30 years. OU-4 Alternative 3 permanently removes contaminated soils and restores ecological function.

*4. Reduction of Toxicity, Mobility, or Volume Through Treatment.* The Selected Remedy significantly reduces the toxicity, mobility, and volume of hazardous substances through thermal desorption (OU-1), pump-and-treat with AOP treatment (OU-3), and in-situ ERD (OU-3). The OU-2 Selected Remedy relies primarily on containment rather than treatment but includes leachate treatment. The Selected Remedy satisfies the statutory preference for treatment as a principal element.

*5. Short-Term Effectiveness.* The Selected Remedy alternatives involve significant construction activities that will generate short-term impacts, including dust, noise, and truck traffic. These impacts will be mitigated through implementation of the Community Air Monitoring Plan, dust suppression measures, designated haul routes, and health and safety protocols. Construction durations are estimated at 2 to 3 years for OU-1 and OU-2, with groundwater treatment operations extending over the 30-year remedial timeframe.

*6. Implementability.* The Selected Remedy technologies are commercially available and have been successfully implemented at comparable Superfund sites. Steam-enhanced extraction and thermal desorption are proven technologies for DNAPL recovery and soil treatment. AOP using UV/hydrogen peroxide is a well-established technology for 1,4-dioxane treatment. The on-site containment cell for OU-2 uses standard geotechnical construction methods.

*7. Cost.* The total present-value cost of the Selected Remedy is \$89.4 million. While not the least costly option for each OU, the Selected Remedy represents a cost-effective balance between protectiveness and expenditure. For OU-1, the Selected Remedy (\$31.2M) is substantially less expensive than full excavation and off-site disposal (\$48.5M) while achieving comparable protectiveness. For OU-3, the Selected Remedy (\$28.9M) is significantly less expensive than in-situ thermal treatment (\$112.6M) and more effective than pump-and-treat only (\$21.3M).

**Modifying Criteria:**

*8. State Acceptance.* The Ohio EPA concurs with the Selected Remedy, as documented in the State Concurrence Letter dated September 10, 2021 (see Appendix C).

*9. Community Acceptance.* The majority of public comments received during the comment period expressed support for an aggressive cleanup approach consistent with the Selected Remedy. Community members emphasized the importance of protecting the Ashford County public water supply wellfield and restoring Millhaven Creek. Specific community concerns regarding air quality and truck traffic are addressed through the CAMP and designated haul route provisions of the Selected Remedy. See Part 3 (Responsiveness Summary) for a detailed discussion of community comments.

**[2.11 Principal Threat Wastes]{.underline}**

EPA guidance (OSWER Directive 9380.3-06FS, \"A Guide to Principal Threat and Low Level Threat Wastes\") identifies principal threat wastes as source materials that include or contain hazardous substances at concentrations and in forms that are highly toxic, highly mobile, or that cannot be reliably contained. The NCP expresses a general expectation that treatment will be used to address principal threat wastes.

At the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site, the following materials are classified as principal threat wastes:

> • **DNAPL in the OU-1 source zone:** The DNAPL, consisting primarily of TCE, is present as a mobile non-aqueous phase liquid at concentrations representing essentially pure product. The DNAPL is the primary ongoing source of dissolved-phase groundwater contamination and cannot be reliably contained through engineering controls alone due to its density-driven downward migration potential.
>
> • **Highly contaminated lagoon materials in OU-2:** The lagoon sediments contain elevated concentrations of multiple hazardous substances and represent an ongoing source of contamination to the shallow aquifer.

The Selected Remedy addresses principal threat wastes through thermal desorption treatment of OU-1 soils and DNAPL recovery via steam-enhanced extraction, and through excavation and engineered containment with leachate treatment for OU-2 lagoon materials.

**[2.12 Selected Remedy]{.underline}**

**2.12.1 Summary of the Selected Remedy**

The Selected Remedy for the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site is a comprehensive, multi-component remedial action that addresses contamination across all four operable units through a combination of source removal, treatment, containment, in-situ bioremediation, pump-and-treat, institutional controls, and ecological restoration. The Selected Remedy achieves cleanup through both active remediation and long-term management and is designed to achieve the remedial action objectives established for each operable unit within the timeframes specified in Section 2.8 of this ROD.

The total estimated present-value cost of the Selected Remedy is **\$89.4 million**, broken down by operable unit as follows:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Operable Unit**                   **Present-Value Cost**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  OU-1: Former Production Area        \$31.2 million

  OU-2: Wastewater Lagoon Area        \$18.7 million

  OU-3: Groundwater Plume             \$28.9 million

  OU-4: Riparian Corridor             \$10.6 million

  **Total**                           **\$89.4 million**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

The remedy components for each operable unit are described in detail in the following subsections.

**2.12.2 OU-1 Selected Remedy: Excavation, Thermal Desorption, and DNAPL Recovery**

The Selected Remedy for OU-1 consists of the following components:

**Soil Excavation.** Excavation of contaminated soils exceeding industrial PRGs to a depth of 15 feet below ground surface (bgs). Excavation shall extend to a minimum depth of 15 feet bgs across the OU-1 area to ensure removal of all soils contaminated above industrial PRGs, based on the vertical extent of contamination documented in the RI. The estimated excavation volume is 42,000 cubic yards. Excavation boundaries shall be confirmed through field screening and confirmatory sampling during remedial construction. Excavation sidewall and bottom confirmatory samples shall be collected and analyzed to verify that all soils exceeding industrial PRGs have been removed to the specified depth.

**DNAPL Recovery.** DNAPL recovery shall be accomplished via steam-enhanced extraction (SEE) using injection/extraction well pairs installed across the 3.5-acre DNAPL source zone. A minimum of 14 injection/extraction well pairs shall be installed to ensure adequate steam distribution and DNAPL mobilization across the full extent of the source zone. The SEE system shall inject steam into the subsurface through injection wells to heat the DNAPL zone, reducing DNAPL viscosity and increasing its mobility toward extraction wells where it can be recovered. Extracted fluids (DNAPL, steam condensate, and groundwater) shall be treated at the on-site groundwater treatment plant prior to discharge. The SEE system design shall be refined during remedial design based on additional characterization data and pilot testing, but shall maintain the minimum of 14 injection/extraction well pairs specified in this ROD. Performance monitoring shall include measurement of DNAPL recovery rates, subsurface temperature distribution, and dissolved-phase contaminant concentrations in extraction well effluent and surrounding monitoring wells. DNAPL recovery operations shall continue until either (a) asymptotic mass recovery rates are achieved, indicating that the recoverable DNAPL mass has been substantially addressed, or (b) dissolved-phase contaminant concentrations in monitoring wells demonstrate a declining trend consistent with achievement of groundwater RAOs within the 30-year timeframe.

**Ex-Situ Thermal Desorption.** Excavated soils shall undergo ex-situ thermal desorption to volatilize and destroy organic contaminants. The treatment standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs applies to all treated soils regardless of intended reuse, including soils designated for on-site backfill, to ensure long-term protectiveness and prevent recontamination of the subsurface. Treated soils meeting the 1 mg/kg treatment standard may be used as backfill on-site within the OU-1 excavation area. Soils that do not meet the 1 mg/kg treatment standard after thermal desorption shall be characterized, manifested, and transported for off-site disposal at a RCRA Subtitle C facility in accordance with applicable RCRA land disposal restrictions (40 CFR Part 268). Treatment residuals, including off-gas condensate and baghouse dust, shall be characterized and disposed of in accordance with applicable regulations.

**Institutional Controls.** Institutional controls shall be implemented to restrict future land use at OU-1 to industrial and commercial purposes. The institutional controls shall be memorialized through an environmental covenant recorded with the Ashford County Recorder\'s Office, prohibiting residential land use, restricting subsurface intrusion activities without prior EPA approval, and prohibiting installation of groundwater extraction wells for potable use. The institutional controls shall remain in effect until such time as EPA determines that unrestricted use and unlimited exposure conditions have been achieved.

**Estimated Cost.** The estimated present-value cost for the OU-1 Selected Remedy is \$31.2 million.

**2.12.3 OU-2 Selected Remedy: Excavation and On-Site Containment**

The Selected Remedy for OU-2 consists of the following components:

**Excavation.** Excavation and removal of lagoon sediments and contaminated underlying soils to the native clay layer, identified in the RI at approximately 12 feet bgs. Excavation shall extend to the native clay layer to ensure complete removal of contaminated materials above the natural confining unit. The estimated excavation volume is 28,500 cubic yards. Excavation shall encompass all three former lagoon areas and surrounding buffer zones where contamination has migrated laterally beyond the lagoon footprints. Confirmatory sampling of the exposed native clay surface shall be conducted to verify that all contaminated materials above the confining unit have been removed. Any contamination identified within the upper portion of the native clay layer shall be evaluated during remedial design, and additional removal shall be performed as necessary to ensure protectiveness.

**On-Site Engineered Containment Cell.** Excavated lagoon materials shall be consolidated in an on-site engineered containment cell constructed on the Site property at a location to be determined during remedial design. The containment cell shall be designed and constructed with the following specifications:

> • **Composite Liner System:** The composite liner system shall comply with the substantive requirements of 40 CFR 264.310 for landfill closure, including a minimum 60-mil HDPE geomembrane over a minimum 24-inch (2-foot) compacted clay liner. The compacted clay component shall achieve a maximum hydraulic conductivity of 1 × 10⁻⁷ cm/sec. The HDPE geomembrane shall be installed in accordance with the manufacturer\'s specifications and shall be seam-tested using vacuum and air-pressure testing methods to verify integrity. A geocomposite drainage layer shall be installed above the HDPE liner to facilitate leachate collection.
>
> • **RCRA-Equivalent Cap:** A RCRA-equivalent cap meeting the substantive requirements of 40 CFR 264.310 shall be installed over the containment cell following placement and compaction of lagoon materials. The cap shall include, at a minimum, an infiltration barrier layer, a drainage layer, and a vegetative soil cover designed to minimize long-term maintenance requirements and promote stormwater runoff.

**Leachate Collection and Treatment System.** A leachate collection and treatment system shall be installed within the containment cell to collect any leachate generated from the contained materials. Leachate collected from the containment cell shall be conveyed to the on-site groundwater treatment plant for treatment prior to discharge under the site NPDES permit. The leachate collection system shall include a sump, conveyance piping, and a leachate holding tank of adequate capacity to manage anticipated leachate generation rates. Leachate generation rates shall be monitored, and the system shall be maintained to ensure continuous operation throughout the post-closure monitoring period.

**Long-Term Groundwater Monitoring.** A minimum of 8 monitoring wells shall be installed downgradient of the containment cell. Monitoring shall be conducted quarterly for the first 5 years following containment cell construction, transitioning to semi-annual monitoring thereafter, subject to EPA approval. Monitoring parameters shall include the full suite of OU-2 contaminants of concern, leachate indicator parameters, and water level measurements. The monitoring program shall be designed to detect any release from the containment cell and to verify that the containment system remains protective of groundwater quality.

**Estimated Cost.** The estimated present-value cost for the OU-2 Selected Remedy is \$18.7 million.

**2.12.4 OU-3 Selected Remedy: Pump-and-Treat with In-Situ ERD and AOP Treatment**

The Selected Remedy for OU-3 consists of the following components:

**Pump-and-Treat Extraction System.** The extraction system shall consist of a minimum of 12 extraction wells along an extraction trench of no less than 2,400 linear feet to ensure hydraulic capture of the full width of the plume and prevent bypassing of contaminated groundwater toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield. The extraction trench shall be aligned perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow at the downgradient margin of the dissolved-phase contaminant plume. The extraction wells shall be screened across the full saturated thickness of the shallow aquifer and shall be pumped at rates sufficient to create an inward hydraulic gradient across the full width of the plume. The extraction system shall be designed to achieve a minimum capture zone width equal to the plume width plus an additional 200 feet on each lateral margin to account for seasonal variations in groundwater flow direction and plume geometry. Groundwater flow modeling shall be performed during remedial design to optimize well spacing, pumping rates, and trench alignment. Capture zone analysis shall be performed quarterly using water level data from the monitoring well network to verify that the extraction system is achieving full hydraulic capture.

**On-Site Groundwater Treatment Plant.** An on-site groundwater treatment plant shall be constructed to treat extracted groundwater and leachate from the OU-2 containment cell. The treatment plant shall include the following treatment train:

> • **Air Stripping:** A packed-tower air stripper shall be used as the primary treatment unit for removal of volatile chlorinated compounds, including TCE and PCE, from extracted groundwater. The air stripper shall be designed to achieve effluent concentrations below applicable NPDES permit limits for chlorinated VOCs. Off-gas from the air stripper shall be treated through vapor-phase granular activated carbon prior to atmospheric discharge in compliance with applicable air quality requirements.
>
> • **Granular Activated Carbon (GAC) Polishing:** Liquid-phase granular activated carbon adsorption units shall be installed downstream of the air stripper to remove residual organic compounds that are not completely removed by air stripping. The GAC system shall be configured in a lead-lag series arrangement to ensure continuous treatment and to allow carbon change-out without interrupting operations.
>
> • **Advanced Oxidation Process (AOP) for 1,4-Dioxane:** An advanced oxidation process (AOP) unit utilizing ultraviolet (UV) light and hydrogen peroxide shall be included in the treatment train specifically for the destruction of 1,4-dioxane. 1,4-Dioxane is resistant to conventional adsorption on granular activated carbon due to its high water solubility and low octanol-water partition coefficient (log Kow = −0.27), making GAC alone an inadequate treatment technology for this contaminant. The low Henry\'s Law constant of 1,4-dioxane similarly renders air stripping ineffective for its removal. The AOP unit is an essential component of the treatment system to achieve the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level of 0.35 µg/L. The AOP system shall be designed to achieve a minimum 1,4-dioxane destruction efficiency of 99 percent and shall reduce 1,4-dioxane concentrations in treated effluent to below the NPDES permit limit and the groundwater cleanup level of 0.35 µg/L.

**Treated Water Discharge.** Treated water from the groundwater treatment plant shall be discharged to Millhaven Creek under an NPDES permit issued by the Ohio EPA. The NPDES permit shall specify effluent limits consistent with Ohio Water Quality Standards and applicable federal requirements. Effluent monitoring shall be conducted in accordance with the NPDES permit conditions to verify compliance with all discharge limits.

**In-Situ Enhanced Reductive Dechlorination (ERD).** In-situ enhanced reductive dechlorination (ERD) shall be implemented in the mid-plume area to accelerate biodegradation of dissolved chlorinated solvents (TCE and PCE) and their transformation products (cis-1,2-dichloroethylene and vinyl chloride). The ERD program shall involve injection of an emulsified vegetable oil (EVO) substrate to create anaerobic conditions conducive to reductive dechlorination by indigenous or bioaugmented dehalorespiring microorganisms (e.g., Dehalococcoides spp.).

The ERD injection grid shall consist of a minimum of 48 injection points at 30-foot center-to-center spacing to ensure adequate substrate distribution and biological activity across the mid-plume treatment zone. The injection grid shall be located in the mid-plume area, between the source zone and the extraction trench, to treat the highest concentrations of dissolved chlorinated solvents within the plume. Initial injection events shall deliver EVO substrate at a dosing rate sufficient to achieve a target electron donor-to-electron acceptor ratio of at least 5:1 in the treatment zone. Subsequent re-injection events shall be scheduled based on performance monitoring results, and shall occur at intervals of approximately 12 to 18 months or as determined by the remedial design/remedial action work plan. Performance monitoring within the ERD treatment zone shall include sampling for parent compounds (TCE, PCE), daughter products (cis-1,2-DCE, vinyl chloride, ethene, ethane), geochemical parameters (dissolved oxygen, oxidation-reduction potential, pH, dissolved iron, sulfate, methane), and molecular biological tools (quantitative polymerase chain reaction for Dehalococcoides spp.).

**Groundwater Cleanup Levels.** The following groundwater cleanup levels shall apply at point of compliance wells located at the Site boundary:

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Contaminant**             **Cleanup Level**       **Basis**
  --------------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------------------------------
  Trichloroethylene (TCE)     5 µg/L                  Federal MCL (40 CFR 141.61)

  Tetrachloroethylene (PCE)   5 µg/L                  Federal MCL (40 CFR 141.61)

  1,4-Dioxane                 0.35 µg/L               EPA Health Advisory Level

  Hexavalent Chromium         100 µg/L                Federal MCL for total chromium (40 CFR 141.61)
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The cleanup level for 1,4-dioxane is established at 0.35 µg/L, based on the EPA Health Advisory Level, which EPA has determined to be the most protective and appropriate standard for this site. This value is more stringent than the Ohio EPA generic screening level and is selected based on site-specific risk assessment findings and the proximity of the Ashford County public water supply wellfield.

**Monitoring Well Network.** A monitoring well network of no fewer than 36 monitoring wells shall be established across the plume to assess remedy performance and protectiveness. Monitoring shall be conducted quarterly for the first 3 years of system operation, transitioning to semi-annual monitoring thereafter. The remedy shall be deemed to have achieved cleanup levels when all point of compliance wells demonstrate attainment of cleanup levels for 8 consecutive semi-annual sampling rounds. The monitoring well network shall include wells distributed across the plume from the source area to the downgradient leading edge, including wells between the extraction trench and the Ashford County public water supply wellfield to provide early detection of any plume bypassing.

**Performance Timeline.** Based on the FS modeling, the Selected Remedy is projected to achieve groundwater RAOs within approximately 30 years of initial system startup. This estimate is based on assumptions regarding contaminant mass removal rates, in-situ treatment effectiveness, and natural attenuation contributions, and will be refined as actual performance data are obtained during system operation. Five-year reviews will evaluate whether the remedy is on track to meet the 30-year timeline and will recommend modifications as warranted.

**Estimated Cost.** The estimated present-value cost for the OU-3 Selected Remedy is \$28.9 million.

**2.12.5 OU-4 Selected Remedy: Excavation and Ecological Restoration**

The Selected Remedy for OU-4 consists of the following components:

**Excavation of Contaminated Floodplain Soils.** Contaminated floodplain soils exceeding ecological risk-based screening levels shall be excavated to a depth of 3 feet bgs along the 4.5-acre riparian corridor of Millhaven Creek south of the main facility area. The estimated excavation volume is 6,800 cubic yards. Excavation limits shall be based on the ecological risk-based screening levels developed during the RI/BERA, refined by pre-construction confirmation sampling. Excavation activities within the floodplain shall be scheduled to avoid the fish spawning season (April through June) and shall incorporate best management practices to minimize sedimentation and disturbance to Millhaven Creek, including installation of silt fencing, turbidity curtains, and temporary stream diversions as needed.

**Ecological Restoration.** Excavated areas shall be restored with clean fill, topsoil, and native riparian vegetation in accordance with a Habitat Restoration Plan to be developed by the PRP\'s environmental consultant and submitted for review and approval. The Habitat Restoration Plan shall be submitted for review and approval by both the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and the Ohio Department of Natural Resources (ODNR). Both agencies shall serve as co-approvers of the plan to ensure compliance with federal and state ecological protection requirements. The Habitat Restoration Plan shall specify, at a minimum: target plant community composition, including species mix, planting densities, and planting methods; soil amendment and grading requirements; erosion and sediment control measures during and after planting; an adaptive management strategy to address contingencies such as plant mortality, invasive species encroachment, and erosion; and performance criteria for vegetation establishment.

**Ecological Monitoring Program.** A minimum 5-year ecological monitoring program shall be conducted following completion of restoration activities. The monitoring program shall include: (a) annual benthic macroinvertebrate surveys in Millhaven Creek adjacent to and downstream of the restored area, using the same protocols and reference stations employed during the RI baseline surveys; (b) quarterly surface water quality monitoring at established stations upstream, within, and downstream of the restored area for the OU-4 contaminants of concern; and (c) annual vegetation survival assessments to evaluate establishment and health of planted riparian species, including percent cover, species diversity, and comparison to performance criteria established in the Habitat Restoration Plan. Results shall be reported annually to EPA and USFWS/ODNR. The ecological monitoring program shall include contingency provisions for supplemental planting or other corrective measures if vegetation performance criteria are not met within the 5-year monitoring period.

**Estimated Cost.** The estimated present-value cost for the OU-4 Selected Remedy is \$10.6 million.

**2.12.6 Cross-Cutting Remedy Components**

The following cross-cutting requirements apply to the Selected Remedy across all operable units:

**Community Air Monitoring Plan (CAMP).** A Community Air Monitoring Plan (CAMP) shall be implemented during all intrusive field activities at the Site, including excavation, soil loading and hauling, thermal desorption operations, and any other activities with the potential to generate airborne contaminants. The CAMP shall include real-time perimeter air monitoring with the following action levels:

> • Particulate matter (PM-10): 150 µg/m³ (15-minute average at fenceline monitoring stations)
>
> • Total volatile organic compounds (VOCs): 5 ppmv (15-minute average at fenceline monitoring stations)

If action levels are exceeded, work shall cease and corrective measures shall be implemented before resuming activities. Corrective measures may include enhanced dust suppression (water misting, application of foam suppressants), reduction in excavation rates, installation of temporary enclosures, or other engineering controls appropriate to the specific conditions. CAMP data shall be reported to EPA and made available to the community through regular updates to the Millhaven Community Advisory Group.

**Transportation and Haul Routes.** Transportation of contaminated materials, debris, and other remediation wastes shall be conducted via designated haul routes that avoid residential areas. The designated haul route shall be State Route 47 to Interstate 71. No haul traffic shall be routed through residential neighborhoods, including Millhaven Heights or any other residential area. All haul vehicles shall be covered or enclosed to prevent release of materials during transport. A traffic management plan shall be developed during remedial design and shall include provisions for maintaining roadway safety, minimizing traffic congestion, and coordinating with local authorities regarding road conditions and any temporary road closures.

**Health and Safety Plan (HASP).** A site-specific Health and Safety Plan (HASP) shall be prepared and maintained in compliance with 29 CFR 1910.120 (OSHA Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response --- HAZWOPER). All on-site workers shall receive HAZWOPER training as required by 29 CFR 1910.120(e), including initial 40-hour HAZWOPER training for general site workers, 8-hour annual refresher training, and additional site-specific training addressing the specific hazards associated with the Hargrove Industrial Complex site. The HASP shall establish exclusion zones, contamination reduction zones, and support zones; specify personal protective equipment requirements; define medical surveillance requirements; and include emergency response procedures, including provisions for coordination with local fire and emergency medical services.

**Applicable or Relevant and Appropriate Requirements (ARARs).** The Selected Remedy shall comply with all applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements (ARARs) identified in the ARARs analysis (see Section 2.13 and Table 2-1). A total of 47 ARARs have been identified for the Selected Remedy, encompassing chemical-specific ARARs (establishing cleanup levels and discharge standards), action-specific ARARs (governing the methods and practices used to implement the remedy), and location-specific ARARs (addressing the physical and ecological characteristics of the Site and surrounding area). Compliance with each identified ARAR is described in the ARARs Compliance Matrix (Table 2-1).

**Performance Standards and Timeframes.** The Selected Remedy shall achieve Remedial Action Objectives within 30 years for groundwater cleanup and 5 years for soil and source area cleanup, measured from commencement of active remediation. These timeframes represent the performance standards against which remedy effectiveness will be measured during five-year reviews.

**Five-Year Review.** Pursuant to CERCLA Section 121(c), 42 U.S.C. § 9621(c), five-year reviews shall be conducted to evaluate whether the remedy remains protective of human health and the environment. Because the Selected Remedy will result in hazardous substances remaining on-site above levels that allow for unlimited use and unrestricted exposure, the first Five-Year Review is due September 2026 (five years after ROD issuance). Subsequent five-year reviews shall be conducted at intervals of no more than five years until EPA determines that the remedy is protective and no further reviews are necessary.

**Institutional Controls.** A comprehensive institutional controls program shall be implemented across the Site to supplement the engineering components of the remedy. The institutional controls program shall include: (a) environmental covenants recorded with the Ashford County Recorder\'s Office restricting land use to industrial/commercial purposes; (b) groundwater use restrictions prohibiting installation of drinking water wells on the Site property and within the plume boundary; (c) excavation and subsurface intrusion restrictions requiring prior EPA notification and approval for any ground-disturbing activities at the Site; and (d) periodic inspection and reporting to verify that institutional controls remain in place and are being enforced. The institutional controls shall be enforceable by EPA under the Consent Decree and by the State of Ohio under applicable state law.

**[2.13 Applicable or Relevant and Appropriate Requirements (ARARs)]{.underline}**

**2.13.1 Introduction to ARARs**

Section 121(d) of CERCLA, 42 U.S.C. § 9621(d), requires that remedial actions at Superfund sites attain, or provide a basis for invoking a waiver of, applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements (ARARs) under federal and state environmental laws. ARARs are categorized as follows:

> • **Applicable requirements** are those cleanup standards, standards of control, and other substantive environmental protection requirements, criteria, or limitations promulgated under federal or state environmental or facility siting laws that specifically address a hazardous substance, pollutant, contaminant, remedial action, location, or other circumstance found at a CERCLA site.
>
> • **Relevant and appropriate requirements** are those cleanup standards, standards of control, and other substantive requirements, criteria, or limitations promulgated under federal or state environmental or facility siting laws that, while not \"applicable\" to a hazardous substance, pollutant, contaminant, remedial action, location, or other circumstance at a CERCLA site, address problems or situations sufficiently similar to those encountered at the site that their use is well suited to the particular site.

ARARs are further categorized as chemical-specific (establishing concentration limits or risk levels for specific contaminants), action-specific (governing the performance or design of specific remedial activities), and location-specific (relating to the geographic or physical characteristics of the site and surrounding area).

A total of 47 ARARs have been identified for the Selected Remedy at the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site. The Selected Remedy shall attain all identified ARARs. No ARAR waivers are invoked in this ROD. The complete ARARs Compliance Matrix is presented in Table 2-1 below.

Capital costs include the costs of site preparation, construction, equipment procurement and installation, contractor mobilization, engineering oversight, and project management.
