**[2.15 Expected Outcomes of the Selected Remedy]{.underline}**

Implementation of the Selected Remedy is expected to achieve the following outcomes:

**OU-1: Former Production Area.** Excavation and thermal desorption will remove approximately 42,000 cubic yards of contaminated soils and destroy organic contaminants to a treatment standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs. DNAPL recovery via steam-enhanced extraction will significantly reduce the mass of non-aqueous phase liquid in the source zone, thereby reducing the ongoing flux of dissolved contaminants to groundwater. The OU-1 area will be available for industrial reuse following completion of soil remediation, anticipated within 5 years of construction commencement.

**OU-2: Wastewater Lagoon Area.** Excavation and on-site containment will remove contaminated lagoon materials from direct contact with the shallow aquifer and consolidate them in an engineered containment cell meeting RCRA-equivalent standards. The containment system, combined with leachate collection and treatment, will eliminate the ongoing contribution of contaminants from the lagoon area to groundwater. Long-term monitoring will verify protectiveness of the containment system.

**OU-3: Groundwater Plume.** The combined pump-and-treat, AOP treatment, and in-situ ERD remedy is projected to restore groundwater to cleanup levels within approximately 30 years of initial system startup. The extraction system will prevent further migration of the plume toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield, thereby protecting the drinking water supply for approximately 14,000 residents. Treated water will be discharged to Millhaven Creek in compliance with NPDES permit limits, contributing to flow maintenance in the stream.

**OU-4: Riparian Corridor.** Excavation of contaminated floodplain soils and ecological restoration will restore the 4.5-acre riparian corridor to support native ecological communities, including benthic macroinvertebrate populations and riparian vegetation. Attainment of ecological screening levels in floodplain soils is expected upon completion of excavation. Ecological monitoring will verify the success of the restoration effort over a 5-year period.

Overall, the Selected Remedy is protective of human health and the environment and will achieve cleanup levels within the timeframes established in the remedial action objectives. The remedy addresses principal threat wastes through treatment, utilizes permanent solutions to the maximum extent practicable, and satisfies the statutory preference for treatment.

**[PART 3: RESPONSIVENESS SUMMARY]{.underline}**

**[3.1 Overview of Public Participation Process]{.underline}**

EPA conducted an extensive public participation process for the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site in accordance with the requirements of CERCLA Section 117 and the NCP. The Proposed Plan was released on June 15, 2021, and presented EPA\'s preferred remedy for the Site. An initial 30-day public comment period ran from June 15 through July 15, 2021. In response to requests from community members and the Millhaven Community Advisory Group (CAG), EPA extended the public comment period by an additional 15 days, to July 30, 2021.

A public meeting was held at the Millhaven Community Center on June 28, 2021, attended by approximately 85 community members. At the public meeting, Dr. Sandra Volkov, EPA Remedial Project Manager, and other EPA technical staff presented the Proposed Plan, explained the alternatives evaluated, and answered questions from attendees. Ellen Dorsey, Chairperson of the Millhaven Community Advisory Group, facilitated community discussion at the meeting.

During the comment period, EPA received written comments from 43 individuals, the Millhaven Community Advisory Group, Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc., the Ohio EPA, and other stakeholders. All significant comments received are summarized below, together with EPA\'s responses.

**[3.2 Summary of Significant Comments and Responses]{.underline}**

**3.2.1 Community Concerns --- Remedy Protectiveness and Timeliness**

**Summary of Comments:** Multiple community members and the Millhaven Community Advisory Group submitted comments expressing strong support for an aggressive cleanup approach and urging EPA to prioritize the most protective remedy. The CAG, through Chairperson Ellen Dorsey, submitted a letter emphasizing that the community has lived with the effects of contamination for decades and that EPA should select the remedy that achieves the fastest and most thorough cleanup possible. Several commenters expressed concern that the 30-year groundwater cleanup timeline is too long and requested that EPA commit to accelerating the timeline if feasible. Commenters also emphasized the critical importance of protecting the Ashford County public water supply wellfield.

**EPA Response:** EPA appreciates the community\'s engagement and shares the commitment to achieving the most protective cleanup achievable. The Selected Remedy (Alternative 3 for OU-1, Alternative 3 for OU-2, Alternative 4 for OU-3, and Alternative 3 for OU-4) represents the most protective cost-effective alternative for each operable unit and will achieve remedial action objectives within the stated timeframes. The 30-year groundwater cleanup timeline is based on the best available modeling projections and represents an aggressive remediation approach that combines pump-and-treat, advanced oxidation, and in-situ bioremediation. EPA will evaluate actual remedy performance during five-year reviews and will pursue opportunities to accelerate the cleanup timeline if performance data support such acceleration.

**3.2.2 Community Concerns --- Air Quality and Truck Traffic**

**Summary of Comments:** Numerous comments were received expressing concern about potential air quality impacts and truck traffic during excavation and construction activities. Residents of Millhaven Heights, located southeast of the Site, were particularly concerned about dust emissions, volatile organic compound releases, and the routing of heavy haul trucks through residential streets. The CAG submitted comments requesting that EPA require strict air monitoring standards and designate haul routes that avoid all residential neighborhoods.

**EPA Response:** EPA has incorporated robust air quality protection and traffic management measures into the Selected Remedy. The Community Air Monitoring Plan (CAMP) will be implemented during all intrusive field activities and will include real-time perimeter air monitoring at fenceline stations. The CAMP action levels are: particulate matter (PM-10) at 150 µg/m³ (15-minute average) and total volatile organic compounds (VOCs) at 5 ppmv (15-minute average). If either action level is exceeded, work will cease and corrective measures will be implemented before resuming activities. Regarding truck traffic, the Selected Remedy specifies that the designated haul route shall be State Route 47 to Interstate 71. No haul traffic shall be routed through residential neighborhoods, including Millhaven Heights. These measures are designed to protect community health and minimize disruption to residents during the remedial action.

**3.2.3 Community Concerns --- Wellfield Protection**

**Summary of Comments:** Several comments were received from community members and the Ashford County Water Department expressing concern about the protection of the Ashford County public water supply wellfield, which serves approximately 14,000 residents and is located 1.8 miles downgradient of the leading edge of the groundwater plume. Commenters requested assurance that the Selected Remedy would prevent contamination from reaching the wellfield.

**EPA Response:** Protection of the Ashford County public water supply wellfield is a primary objective of the OU-3 Selected Remedy. The pump-and-treat extraction system, consisting of 12 extraction wells along a 2,400-foot extraction trench at the downgradient margin of the plume, is specifically designed to achieve hydraulic capture of the full plume width and prevent any further migration of contaminated groundwater toward the wellfield. The monitoring well network, which includes wells between the extraction trench and the wellfield, will provide early detection capability in the unlikely event of plume bypassing. Groundwater monitoring will be conducted quarterly for the first 3 years, providing frequent data to verify extraction system performance. EPA is committed to maintaining the protectiveness of the extraction system throughout the remedial action and will adjust pumping rates and well configurations as needed based on monitoring data.

**3.2.4 Comments from CCH**

**Summary of Comments:** Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc. (CCH), through its General Counsel Patricia Eng and VP of Environmental Compliance Derek Yamashita, submitted comments generally supporting the Selected Remedy. CCH expressed its commitment to performing the remedial design and remedial action in accordance with the Consent Decree. CCH requested flexibility in the implementation of certain remedy components during the remedial design phase, noting that additional site characterization data collected during remedial design may warrant optimization of certain design specifications, such as well locations, injection point spacing, and treatment system sizing.

**EPA Response:** EPA appreciates CCH\'s commitment to implementing the Selected Remedy. EPA recognizes that remedial design is an iterative process in which additional site characterization data may inform optimization of specific design elements. However, any modifications to the ROD-specified remedy must follow the established modification procedures. Non-significant changes to the remedy may be documented through an Explanation of Significant Differences (ESD). Significant or fundamental changes to the remedy require a ROD Amendment with public participation. All modifications must be consistent with the overall protectiveness and performance standards established in this ROD. The Consent Decree (Case No. 3:20-cv-00487-JHR, N.D. Ohio) governs the remedial design and remedial action implementation process and provides the framework for EPA oversight and approval of design submittals.

**3.2.5 Comments from Ohio EPA**

**Summary of Comments:** The Ohio Environmental Protection Agency submitted comments expressing concurrence with the Selected Remedy. Ohio EPA emphasized the importance of establishing the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level at 0.35 µg/L based on the EPA Health Advisory Level, noting that this standard is more stringent than Ohio\'s generic screening level and is warranted by the site-specific risk assessment findings and the proximity of the Ashford County public water supply wellfield. Ohio EPA also expressed strong support for the inclusion of the AOP treatment technology in the OU-3 treatment train, noting that it is essential for achieving the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level. Additionally, Ohio EPA expressed support for the 5-year ecological monitoring program at OU-4 and for the requirement that both USFWS and ODNR serve as co-approvers of the Habitat Restoration Plan.

**EPA Response:** EPA appreciates Ohio EPA\'s thorough review and concurrence with the Selected Remedy. EPA concurs with Ohio EPA\'s assessment of the importance of the 1,4-dioxane cleanup level, the AOP treatment technology, and the ecological monitoring and agency coordination provisions. These elements are integral to the protectiveness of the Selected Remedy and are reflected in the detailed remedy specifications in Sections 2.12.4 and 2.12.5 of this ROD.

**[3.3 Technical and Legal Comments]{.underline}**

EPA received several additional technical comments from environmental professionals and interested parties. One commenter suggested that in-situ chemical oxidation (ISCO) using sodium persulfate could be a viable alternative to ERD for mid-plume treatment. EPA evaluated ISCO as part of the FS alternatives analysis and determined that while ISCO can be effective for chlorinated solvents, it may generate undesirable byproducts in the presence of 1,4-dioxane and does not provide the sustained biological activity that ERD achieves through substrate injection. ERD was selected because it provides a long-lasting, cost-effective biological treatment barrier in the mid-plume area.

Another commenter requested clarification on the legal framework for enforcement of institutional controls. EPA clarified that institutional controls will be implemented through environmental covenants recorded under Ohio\'s Uniform Environmental Covenants Act (ORC Chapter 5301.80) and will be enforceable by both EPA and the State of Ohio. The Consent Decree provides additional enforcement authority for institutional control compliance.

Two commenters raised questions about the adequacy of the cost estimate, suggesting that actual costs may exceed the \$89.4 million present-value estimate. EPA acknowledges that the cost estimate has an expected accuracy range of +50 percent to −30 percent, consistent with the level of design information available at the FS stage. Costs will be refined during remedial design, and any cost changes will be evaluated in the context of the Consent Decree and applicable cost recovery mechanisms.

**[1.1 Purpose and Scope]{.underline}**

This Remedial Action Work Plan (RAWP) describes the remedial action approach, design specifications, construction procedures, monitoring plans, and operational parameters for the selected remedy at the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site (the \"Site\"), located at 1500 Old Mill Road, Millhaven, Ashford County, Ohio 44078. The RAWP has been prepared by Terraverde Environmental Sciences, LLC (Terraverde) on behalf of Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc. (CCH) in fulfillment of CCH\'s obligations under the Consent Decree entered in the matter of *United States v. Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc.*, Case No. 3:20-cv-00487-JHR, United States District Court, Northern District of Ohio, entered March 2020.

The RAWP addresses all four operable units (OU-1 through OU-4) as defined in the Record of Decision (ROD) issued by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), Region 5, on September 15, 2021. It provides the technical basis for the design and construction of all remedy components, including soil excavation, ex-situ thermal treatment, DNAPL source recovery, engineered containment, groundwater extraction and treatment, in-situ bioremediation, and ecological habitat restoration. In addition, the RAWP presents the long-term monitoring programs, community air monitoring plan, health and safety plan, transportation and materials management plan, and institutional controls associated with the remedial action.

The RAWP is intended to serve as the primary implementation document guiding all remedial activities at the Site. Upon EPA approval, the RAWP will constitute the binding scope of work for remedial action construction and operation. All work will be performed in compliance with the Consent Decree, the ROD, applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements (ARARs), and relevant EPA guidance.

The RAWP includes 14 appendices, bound separately, providing supporting technical data, design drawings, engineering specifications, management plans, and other documentation as described in Section 1.5 of this document.

**[1.2 Site Description and Background]{.underline}**

The Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site is located at 1500 Old Mill Road, Millhaven, Ashford County, Ohio 44078. The Site encompasses approximately 62 acres of former industrial property situated in a mixed-use area of southeastern Ashford County. The Site is bounded to the north by Old Mill Road and agricultural land, to the east by forested land and the Millhaven Heights residential neighborhood, to the south by Millhaven Creek and its associated riparian corridor, and to the west by vacant industrial parcels.

**Historical Operations.** Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. operated the facility from 1954 through 2001, during which time the plant manufactured chlorinated solvents (including trichloroethylene \[TCE\] and tetrachloroethylene \[PCE\]), organic chemical intermediates, and wood-treatment chemicals (including pentachlorophenol \[PCP\]). The manufacturing operations generated process wastewater that was discharged to three unlined lagoons on the southern portion of the property. Storage and handling of bulk chemicals, waste materials, and byproducts occurred throughout the production area. The facility ceased operations in 2001 and the property remained vacant until CCH acquired the assets of Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. through a 2008 asset purchase transaction. CCH is the successor-in-interest and the designated potentially responsible party (PRP) for the Site.

**NPL Listing and Investigation.** The Site was proposed for listing on the National Priorities List (NPL) in March 2016 and was formally listed on September 22, 2016. Terraverde Environmental Sciences, LLC conducted the Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study (RI/FS) on behalf of CCH from 2017 through 2019. The RI/FS was completed and submitted to EPA Region 5 in 2019. The Record of Decision (ROD) was signed by EPA Region 5 on September 15, 2021.

**Operable Units.** The Site has been divided into four operable units, as described below and depicted on Figure 1-2:

> • **OU-1 --- Former Production Area (18 acres):** Encompasses the main manufacturing complex, including former building foundations, tank farm areas, loading docks, and associated infrastructure. Principal contaminants of concern (COCs) in soil include TCE, PCE, PCP (up to 3,200 mg/kg), hexavalent chromium (up to 890 mg/kg), and benzo(a)pyrene (up to 45 mg/kg). DNAPL consisting primarily of chlorinated solvents has been identified in the subsurface within the central portion of OU-1 at depths ranging from 10 to 25 feet below ground surface (bgs).
>
> • **OU-2 --- Wastewater Lagoon Area (8 acres):** Includes three former unlined wastewater lagoons (designated Lagoons A, B, and C) and surrounding impacted soils. Lagoon sediments are contaminated with PCP, chromium, VOCs, and semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs).
>
> • **OU-3 --- Groundwater Plume:** A dissolved-phase contaminant plume approximately 1.2 miles long and 0.4 miles wide, migrating generally southeast through the shallow overburden aquifer. Principal groundwater COCs include TCE (up to 4,800 µg/L; MCL 5 µg/L), PCE (up to 1,250 µg/L; MCL 5 µg/L), 1,4-dioxane (up to 320 µg/L), and hexavalent chromium in localized areas. The Ashford County public water supply wellfield, which serves approximately 14,000 residents, is located approximately 1.8 miles downgradient of the leading edge of the plume.
>
> • **OU-4 --- Riparian Corridor (4.5 acres):** The floodplain and riparian zone along a reach of Millhaven Creek adjacent to the southern boundary of the Site. Contaminated floodplain soils exceed ecological risk-based screening levels for several COCs.

**Surrounding Land Use.** The Site is situated in a transitional area between industrial/commercial properties to the west and residential neighborhoods to the east. The Millhaven Heights residential neighborhood, consisting of approximately 200 single-family homes, is located approximately 0.3 miles east of the Site boundary. Millhaven Creek, a perennial stream classified as a warm-water habitat stream by the Ohio EPA, flows along the southern boundary of the Site (refer to Figures 1-1 and 1-2).

**[1.3 Regulatory Framework]{.underline}**

The remedial action at the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site is being conducted under the authority of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (CERCLA), 42 U.S.C. §§ 9601--9675, as amended by the Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act (SARA). EPA Region 5 serves as the lead federal agency responsible for oversight of the remedial action. The Ohio EPA serves in a support agency role pursuant to a Memorandum of Agreement between EPA Region 5 and Ohio EPA.

The Record of Decision (ROD) for the Site was signed by the EPA Region 5 Regional Administrator on September 15, 2021. The ROD identifies the selected remedy for each operable unit, establishes remedial action objectives (RAOs), defines cleanup standards, and specifies applicable or relevant and appropriate requirements (ARARs). The selected remedy was based on the results of the RI/FS completed by Terraverde in 2019 and on the community participation process conducted during the Proposed Plan comment period.

This RAWP has been prepared pursuant to the Consent Decree entered in the matter of *United States v. Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc.*, Case No. 3:20-cv-00487-JHR, United States District Court, Northern District of Ohio, entered March 2020. Specifically, Section VII, Paragraph 23 of the Consent Decree requires CCH to submit a Remedial Action Work Plan to EPA for review and approval within the timeframes established therein. The Consent Decree further provides for a 60-day EPA review period following submission of the RAWP. Based on the January 15, 2025 submission date, the EPA review period extends from January 28, 2025 through March 28, 2025.

**[Section 2 --- Remedial Action Objectives and Cleanup Standards]{.underline}**

**[2.1 Remedial Action Objectives]{.underline}**

The Remedial Action Objectives (RAOs) for the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site are established in the ROD and define the goals that the remedial action must achieve for each operable unit. The RAOs provide the overarching framework within which all remedy components have been designed. The RAOs for each operable unit are presented below.

**OU-1 --- Former Production Area**

The RAOs for OU-1 are as follows:

1\. Prevent direct contact exposure to contaminated soils by current and future site workers and visitors under the established industrial/commercial land use scenario.

2\. Reduce and remove DNAPL source mass to the maximum extent practicable to mitigate ongoing dissolution and transport of contaminants to groundwater.

3\. Prevent further migration of contaminants from soil sources to groundwater through source removal and treatment.

**OU-2 --- Wastewater Lagoon Area**

The RAOs for OU-2 are as follows:

1\. Prevent direct contact exposure to contaminated lagoon sediments and soils by current and future site workers, visitors, and ecological receptors.

2\. Prevent migration of contaminated materials from the lagoon area to groundwater through excavation and engineered containment of residual materials.

3\. Contain lagoon materials in a manner that is protective of human health and the environment over the long term.

**OU-3 --- Groundwater Plume**

The RAOs for OU-3 are as follows:

1\. Restore groundwater within the contaminant plume to beneficial use by achieving established cleanup levels for all contaminants of concern.

2\. Prevent further migration of the groundwater contaminant plume toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield and Millhaven Creek.

3\. Protect Millhaven Creek and its associated ecological receptors from adverse impacts due to contaminated groundwater discharge.

**OU-4 --- Riparian Corridor**

The RAOs for OU-4 are as follows:

1\. Protect ecological receptors within the riparian corridor from adverse effects associated with contaminated floodplain soils.

2\. Restore the ecological habitat within the riparian corridor to support native plant and wildlife communities.

**Performance Standards.** The ROD establishes that the soil and source area RAOs (OU-1 and OU-2) are to be achieved within 5 years of the initiation of remedial action construction. The groundwater RAOs (OU-3) are to be achieved within 30 years of full-scale remedy operation. Progress toward achievement of RAOs will be evaluated through the performance monitoring programs described in Section 8 and through the Five-Year Reviews required under CERCLA Section 121(c).

**[2.2 Cleanup Standards]{.underline}**

The cleanup standards applicable to the remedial action at the Hargrove Industrial Complex are presented below. These standards define the concentration levels at which the RAOs will be deemed to have been achieved.

**Soil Cleanup Standards**

Soil cleanup standards for OU-1 and OU-2 are based on industrial/commercial Preliminary Remediation Goals (PRGs) for the principal soil COCs, as follows:

> • Pentachlorophenol (PCP): 3.8 mg/kg
>
> • Hexavalent Chromium: 6.3 mg/kg
>
> • Benzo(a)pyrene: 2.1 mg/kg

These PRGs are based on EPA risk assessment methodologies and are protective of human health under the industrial/commercial land use scenario established by the ROD. **Thermal Treatment Standard**

Soils treated by low-temperature thermal desorption (LTTD) shall meet a treatment standard of 5 mg/kg total VOCs prior to reuse as backfill material. This treatment standard is functionally equivalent to the ROD-specified standard given the industrial land use designation of the property and is protective of the backfill reuse scenario. Treated soils meeting this criterion may be placed as backfill within the OU-1 excavation areas as described in Section 3.4.

**[Section 3 --- OU-1: Former Production Area Remedial Action]{.underline}**

**[3.1 Excavation Plan]{.underline}**

OU-1, the Former Production Area, encompasses approximately 18 acres within the central and northern portions of the Site. This area includes the former manufacturing building foundations, chemical storage tank farm, loading and unloading areas, drum storage yards, and associated infrastructure. Contamination within OU-1 consists of chlorinated VOCs (TCE and PCE), pentachlorophenol (PCP), hexavalent chromium, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, including benzo(a)pyrene, in soils and subsurface materials.

The remedial action for OU-1 includes the excavation of contaminated soils exceeding the cleanup standards identified in Section 2.2. Excavation will be conducted to a depth of 12 feet below ground surface (bgs) across the identified contamination footprint. Confirmatory sampling conducted during the 2024 pre-design investigation indicates that contamination in most areas does not extend below 12 feet bgs. The excavation depth has therefore been optimized from the conceptual depth presented in the ROD to reflect site-specific conditions. Detailed PDI boring logs are provided in Appendix A.

**Table 3-1: OU-1 Excavation Parameters**

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Parameter**                       **Value**
  ----------------------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------
  Excavation Area                     18 acres (excavation within defined limits per Figure 3-1)

  Maximum Excavation Depth            12 feet bgs

  Estimated Excavation Volume         38,200 cubic yards

  Treatment Standard (LTTD)           5 mg/kg total VOCs
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Excavation limits are defined by the confirmatory sampling grid established during the PDI and are depicted on Figure 3-1 (Appendix B, Design Drawings). The lateral excavation boundaries have been delineated based on soil analytical data exceeding the applicable PRGs. The excavation will be conducted in a phased sequence, beginning with the former tank farm area (highest contamination) and proceeding to the peripheral areas.

Excavation will be performed using conventional earthmoving equipment, including tracked excavators, front-end loaders, and off-highway dump trucks. Where excavation depths exceed 5 feet bgs, shoring and/or benching will be employed in accordance with OSHA excavation safety requirements (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P). Dewatering will be performed as necessary where excavations encounter the water table, which is typically encountered at approximately 8 to 12 feet bgs within OU-1. Dewatering effluent will be collected and routed to the on-site groundwater treatment plant (Section 7) for treatment prior to discharge.

Confirmatory sampling will be conducted at the excavation sidewalls and bottom at 25-foot intervals along a grid pattern. Samples will be collected and analyzed for VOCs (EPA Method 8260), SVOCs (EPA Method 8270), and metals including hexavalent chromium (EPA Methods 6010/7196) by Clearwater Analytical Laboratories, Inc., Columbus, Ohio. If confirmatory samples indicate that soil concentrations exceed the cleanup standards, additional excavation will be performed in those areas until cleanup levels are achieved or until the practical limits of excavation are reached, as determined by site-specific conditions such as the presence of infrastructure, utilities, or geotechnical constraints.

Soils exceeding cleanup criteria will be segregated and staged for ex-situ thermal treatment as described in Section 3.3. Soils that do not meet the post-treatment criteria after two treatment cycles through the LTTD system will be transported off-site for disposal at Northland Disposal Services, Inc., a RCRA Subtitle C permitted hazardous waste disposal facility located in Seneca County, Ohio.

Institutional controls restricting future land use to industrial/commercial purposes will be implemented as described in Section 3.5 and in the Institutional Controls Plan (Appendix M).

**[3.2 DNAPL Recovery --- Steam-Enhanced Extraction]{.underline}**

The Remedial Investigation identified the presence of dense non-aqueous phase liquid (DNAPL), consisting primarily of chlorinated solvents (TCE and PCE), within the central portion of OU-1. DNAPL has been encountered at depths ranging from approximately 10 to 25 feet bgs, pooled on and within low-permeability horizons within the overburden. The DNAPL source zone, as delineated during the RI and further refined during the 2024 PDI, encompasses an area of approximately 1.5 acres within the former tank farm and production building footprint.

The selected remedy for DNAPL source recovery is steam-enhanced extraction (SEE). The SEE system is designed to mobilize DNAPL through the injection of steam into the subsurface, thereby reducing DNAPL viscosity and enhancing its flow toward extraction wells. The combined injection and extraction of fluids will achieve hydraulic and thermal control of the source zone, enabling recovery of DNAPL mass that would otherwise remain immobile.

The SEE system design consists of 12 injection/extraction well pairs installed across the DNAPL source zone. The well pairs are arranged in a grid pattern with an approximate spacing of 25 feet on center, as depicted on Figure 3-2 (Appendix B, Design Drawings). Each well pair consists of one steam injection well and one multi-phase extraction well. The injection wells will be installed to depths ranging from 15 to 28 feet bgs, screened across the primary DNAPL-bearing intervals. The extraction wells will be installed to similar depths with screen intervals designed to intercept mobilized DNAPL and condensate.

The steam generation facility will be located within the OU-1 construction staging area and will consist of a mobile, skid-mounted boiler system capable of generating steam at temperatures of 250°F to 300°F and pressures up to 30 pounds per square inch gauge (psig). The boiler system will be fueled by natural gas supplied via a temporary utility connection. Steam injection rates will be controlled to maintain subsurface temperatures within the treatment zone while minimizing the potential for uncontrolled DNAPL migration outside the thermal treatment zone. Detailed steam generation and injection system specifications are provided in Appendix C (SEE System Design).

Extracted fluids, consisting of DNAPL, condensate, groundwater, and steam, will be routed through a vapor/liquid separator and then to the on-site groundwater treatment plant (Section 7) for processing. Recovered DNAPL will be collected in dedicated storage tanks and manifested for off-site disposal as hazardous waste at an approved RCRA Subtitle C facility.

Performance monitoring for the SEE system will include the following components:

> • Continuous monitoring of subsurface temperatures using thermocouples installed in monitoring borings within and around the treatment zone.
>
> • Tracking of DNAPL recovery volumes and mass on a weekly basis.
>
> • Periodic groundwater sampling from monitoring wells within and adjacent to the source zone to evaluate dissolved-phase concentrations.
>
> • Pilot testing of the SEE system over a 60-day period prior to full-scale operation to verify design parameters, optimize injection rates, and assess DNAPL mobilization effectiveness.

The SEE system will be operated for a minimum of 18 months, or until asymptotic DNAPL recovery rates are observed, whichever occurs later. Upon completion of the SEE operational period, a technical evaluation of DNAPL source mass reduction will be performed and submitted to EPA for review.

**[3.3 Ex-Situ Thermal Treatment]{.underline}**

Excavated soils from OU-1 that contain VOC contamination above the applicable cleanup standards will be treated using an on-site low-temperature thermal desorption (LTTD) system. The LTTD process involves heating contaminated soils to temperatures sufficient to volatilize organic contaminants, which are then captured and treated in an air pollution control system.

The LTTD unit will be operated at a treatment temperature of 450°F, which has been demonstrated to achieve effective desorption of chlorinated VOCs and semi-volatile organic compounds from comparable soil matrices. The treatment standard for LTTD-treated soils is 5 mg/kg total VOCs. The treatment standard of 5 mg/kg total VOCs is functionally equivalent to more stringent values for the purpose of backfill reuse under the industrial land use designation established for the Site. LTTD at 450°F has been demonstrated to achieve this standard in comparable soil matrices at multiple remediation sites in the Midwest region.

The LTTD system will be a rotary dryer-type unit with a nominal throughput capacity of approximately 25 tons per hour. The system will include the following components:

> • Feed hopper and screening system to remove oversized materials (greater than 2-inch diameter).
>
> • Rotary thermal desorption drum with direct-fired heating.
>
> • Baghouse particulate control system.
>
> • Thermal oxidizer for destruction of desorbed VOCs.
>
> • Condensation and scrubbing system for secondary emissions control.
>
> • Treated soil cooling and discharge conveyor.

All LTTD system emissions will comply with Ohio EPA air quality regulations and applicable National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAPs). An air emissions permit-by-rule or permit-to-install will be obtained from Ohio EPA prior to LTTD system operation. The Thermal Treatment System Design and Emission Control Plan is provided in Appendix D.

Treated soils meeting the 5 mg/kg total VOC treatment standard may be reused as backfill within the OU-1 excavation areas as described in Section 3.4. Confirmatory samples will be collected from each treatment batch at a frequency of one sample per 500 cubic yards and analyzed for total VOCs (EPA Method 8260). Soils that do not meet the treatment standard after two passes through the LTTD system will be loaded for transport and disposed off-site at Northland Disposal Services, Inc. in Seneca County, Ohio.

**[3.4 OU-1 Backfill and Grading]{.underline}**

Following completion of excavation and confirmatory sampling verification, the OU-1 excavation areas will be backfilled and graded to achieve the final surface elevations depicted on Figure 3-3 (Final Grading Plan, Appendix B). Backfill materials will consist of LTTD-treated soils meeting the treatment standard of 5 mg/kg total VOCs, supplemented with clean imported fill as necessary to achieve the required final grades.

Backfill will be placed in lifts not exceeding 12 inches in loose thickness and compacted to a minimum of 95 percent of the maximum dry density as determined by the Standard Proctor Test (ASTM D698). Field density testing will be performed at a frequency of one test per 500 cubic yards of placed fill. The compaction testing program is described in the CQA/CQC Plan (Appendix E).

The final surface grading plan is designed to promote positive drainage away from the former production area and toward the existing stormwater conveyance infrastructure. A stormwater management system consisting of swales, culverts, and a temporary stormwater detention basin will be installed and maintained during and after construction to manage runoff and prevent erosion. The stormwater management design is consistent with Ohio EPA construction stormwater general permit requirements, and a Notice of Intent (NOI) for coverage under the general permit will be filed prior to the initiation of earthwork activities.

**[3.5 OU-1 Institutional Controls]{.underline}**

Institutional controls (ICs) will be implemented for OU-1 to restrict future land use to industrial and commercial purposes, consistent with the ROD. The ICs will consist of an environmental covenant executed pursuant to Ohio Revised Code Chapter 5301.80 et seq. (the Uniform Environmental Covenants Act) and recorded with the Ashford County Recorder\'s Office. The environmental covenant will include the following restrictions:

> • Prohibition on residential land use.
>
> • Prohibition on the installation of water supply wells within the OU-1 area.
>
> • Requirements for soil management during any future subsurface construction activities.

The Institutional Controls Plan is provided in Appendix M.

**[Section 4 --- OU-2: Wastewater Lagoon Area Remedial Action]{.underline}**

**[4.1 Lagoon Sediment and Soil Excavation]{.underline}**

OU-2, the Wastewater Lagoon Area, encompasses approximately 8 acres within the southern portion of the Site. The area includes three former unlined wastewater lagoons designated as Lagoon A (approximately 2.5 acres), Lagoon B (approximately 2.0 acres), and Lagoon C (approximately 1.5 acres), together with surrounding berms and associated impacted soils. The lagoons received process wastewater discharges from the Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. facility throughout its operational history from 1954 to 2001.

The lagoon sediments and contaminated underlying soils contain elevated concentrations of PCP, hexavalent chromium, chlorinated VOCs, and SVOCs. The contamination profile within the lagoon footprints generally consists of a layer of sludge and impacted sediment overlying native alluvial soils.

The remedial action for OU-2 includes excavation of lagoon sediments and contaminated soils to a depth of 10 feet bgs within the footprint of each lagoon and the surrounding impacted area. Sampling conducted during the pre-design investigation indicates that the majority of contamination resides within the upper 10 feet of the subsurface profile. Excavation to this depth will address the principal contaminant mass within the lagoon footprints. PDI boring logs and analytical results supporting this determination are provided in Appendix A.

The estimated total excavation volume for OU-2 is 24,100 cubic yards. Excavation will be conducted using conventional earthmoving equipment. Given the saturated conditions expected within the lower portions of the lagoon excavations, dewatering will be performed as necessary using submersible pumps, with collected water routed to the on-site treatment system.

Excavated lagoon materials will be staged on lined pads within the OU-2 work area prior to placement in the engineered containment cell (Section 4.2). Materials will be covered with polyethylene sheeting during staging to minimize volatile emissions and stormwater infiltration.

Confirmatory sampling of excavation bottoms will be conducted at 50-foot grid intervals. Samples will be analyzed for the full COC suite (VOCs, SVOCs, metals, hexavalent chromium, and PCP) by Clearwater Analytical Laboratories, Inc. If confirmatory results indicate that contamination above cleanup levels remains at the 10-foot bgs excavation depth, additional evaluation and potential further excavation will be considered on a location-specific basis.

**[4.2 Engineered Containment Cell]{.underline}**

Excavated lagoon materials from OU-2 that are not suitable for off-site recycling or treatment will be consolidated in an on-site engineered containment cell located within the northeast portion of the OU-2 area, as depicted on Figure 4-1 (Appendix B). The containment cell is designed to provide long-term isolation of the consolidated lagoon materials from the environment, preventing direct contact exposure and migration of contaminants to groundwater and surface water.

**Table 4-1: OU-2 Containment Cell Design Specifications**

  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Component**                       **Specification**
  ----------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------
  Liner System                        40-mil HDPE geomembrane over 18 inches of compacted clay

  Cap System                          RCRA-equivalent multi-layer cover per 40 CFR 264.310

  Leachate Collection                 Granular drainage layer with HDPE collection piping

  Total Cell Capacity                 Approximately 30,000 cubic yards

  Footprint Area                      Approximately 2.2 acres
  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The containment cell liner system consists of a 40-mil high-density polyethylene (HDPE) geomembrane placed over a minimum 18-inch-thick compacted clay liner. The compacted clay liner will be constructed using on-site or locally sourced clay materials achieving a maximum hydraulic conductivity of 1 × 10⁻⁷ cm/sec. The HDPE geomembrane will be factory-fabricated and field-seamed by certified welding technicians. All field seams will be tested using vacuum box or air pressure testing in accordance with the manufacturer\'s specifications and the CQA/CQC Plan (Appendix E).

The cap system will be constructed following completion of waste placement and will consist of the following layers, from bottom to top:

1\. Grading layer (6 inches minimum compacted soil).

2\. Gas venting layer (12-inch granular layer with passive gas vents, if warranted by gas generation assessments).

3\. 40-mil HDPE geomembrane barrier layer.

4\. Geocomposite drainage layer.

5\. 24-inch protective soil cover.

6\. 6-inch topsoil layer with vegetative cover.

The cap design meets the requirements of 40 CFR 264.310 for RCRA-equivalent closure of hazardous waste landfills. The cap will be graded to promote surface water runoff and prevent ponding. Cap slopes will range from 3 percent to 5 percent. Stormwater runoff from the cap surface will be collected in perimeter drainage channels and routed to the Site stormwater management system.

The geotechnical design of the containment cell, including slope stability analyses, bearing capacity evaluations, and settlement projections, has been performed by Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants, LLC. The geotechnical design report is provided as part of Appendix E (Containment Cell Design and CQA/CQC Plan).

The CQA/CQC program for the containment cell will include observation and testing of all critical construction elements, including clay liner compaction and permeability testing, geomembrane seam testing, drainage layer gradation verification, and cap construction verification. Third-party CQA oversight will be provided throughout the construction period. The CQA/CQC Plan is provided in Appendix E.

**[4.3 Leachate Collection and Management System]{.underline}**

The engineered containment cell will incorporate a leachate collection and removal system (LCRS) designed to collect and remove leachate from the base of the waste mass on a continuous basis. The LCRS consists of the following components:

> • A 12-inch-thick granular drainage layer placed directly above the HDPE liner.
>
> • A network of perforated 6-inch-diameter HDPE collection pipes installed within the drainage layer at a maximum spacing of 50 feet.
>
> • A leachate collection sump located at the low point of the cell floor.
>
> • A submersible pump installed within the sump for leachate extraction.
>
> • Leachate conveyance piping from the sump to a 10,000-gallon double-walled HDPE leachate storage tank.

Collected leachate will be transported for treatment and disposal at the Millhaven Municipal Wastewater Treatment Plant under an industrial pretreatment permit to be obtained pursuant to 40 CFR 403. Prior to the initiation of leachate discharge to the Millhaven facility, a pretreatment permit application will be submitted to the City of Millhaven, and all applicable local pretreatment limits will be met. Leachate characterization sampling will be performed on each tanker load of leachate prior to transport, with analysis for the full COC suite to verify compliance with the pretreatment permit limits.

The estimated long-term leachate generation rate for the containment cell, based on water balance modeling using the Hydrologic Evaluation of Landfill Performance (HELP) model, is approximately 2,500 gallons per month during the initial years following cap construction, declining to approximately 500 gallons per month over the long term as the cap reduces infiltration. The Leachate Management Plan, including the water balance analysis, leachate characterization protocol, and management procedures, is provided in Appendix F.

**[4.4 OU-2 Groundwater Monitoring]{.underline}**

A long-term groundwater monitoring network will be established downgradient of the engineered containment cell to verify the continued effectiveness of the containment system and to detect any potential release of contaminants to groundwater. The monitoring network will consist of 6 monitoring wells installed at locations downgradient of the cell perimeter, with screen intervals spanning the water table and upper saturated zone. Well locations are depicted on Figure 4-1 and detailed in Appendix G (Monitoring Well Installation Details).

Monitoring will be conducted on a quarterly basis for the first 5 years following containment cell construction and cap completion. Following the initial 5-year period, and contingent upon demonstration of stable or declining contaminant concentrations, the monitoring frequency may be reduced to semi-annual with EPA approval.

Groundwater samples will be analyzed for the full COC list, including PCP, total and hexavalent chromium, VOCs (TCE, PCE, vinyl chloride, cis-1,2-dichloroethylene), 1,4-dioxane, and SVOCs. All analytical work will be performed by Clearwater Analytical Laboratories, Inc., Columbus, Ohio, in accordance with the Quality Assurance Project Plan (Appendix N).

Monitoring data will be compiled in semi-annual groundwater monitoring reports and submitted to EPA and Ohio EPA for review.

**[Section 5 --- OU-3: Groundwater Plume Remedial Action]{.underline}**

**[5.1 Plume Delineation and Conceptual Model]{.underline}**

OU-3 encompasses the dissolved-phase groundwater contaminant plume extending from the Site source areas (OU-1 and OU-2) to the southeast through the shallow overburden aquifer. Based on the RI/FS data and the 2024 PDI supplemental monitoring results, the plume extends approximately 1.2 miles in the direction of groundwater flow and approximately 0.4 miles in width, covering an estimated area of approximately 310 acres. The plume originates from the DNAPL source zone within OU-1 and from contaminant leaching from the lagoon area within OU-2.

The principal groundwater contaminants of concern within the plume include:

> • Trichloroethylene (TCE): Maximum detected concentration of 4,800 µg/L in source area wells (MCL: 5 µg/L).
>
> • Tetrachloroethylene (PCE): Maximum detected concentration of 1,250 µg/L in source area wells (MCL: 5 µg/L).
>
> • 1,4-Dioxane: Maximum detected concentration of 320 µg/L in the mid-plume area.
>
> • Hexavalent Chromium: Detected at concentrations exceeding 100 µg/L in localized areas near the lagoon complex.

The contaminant plume is migrating through the shallow overburden aquifer, which consists of glacial outwash sands and gravels with interbedded silt and clay lenses. The aquifer is unconfined to semi-confined, with a saturated thickness of approximately 25 to 40 feet. Groundwater flow is generally to the southeast, consistent with the regional topographic gradient toward Millhaven Creek. Hydraulic conductivity values determined from slug tests and pumping tests conducted during the RI and the 2024 PDI range from 5 × 10⁻⁴ cm/sec to 3 × 10⁻² cm/sec, with a geometric mean of approximately 4 × 10⁻³ cm/sec. The estimated average linear groundwater velocity is approximately 0.5 to 1.5 feet per day.

The Ashford County public water supply wellfield, which serves approximately 14,000 residents, is located approximately 1.8 miles downgradient (southeast) of the current leading edge of the plume. Sentinel monitoring wells installed between the plume leading edge and the wellfield have not detected Site-related contaminants to date.

The groundwater flow and transport model developed during the RI/FS has been updated to incorporate the 2024 PDI data, including revised hydraulic conductivity estimates, updated contaminant distribution data, and refined boundary conditions. The updated model is presented in Appendix I (Groundwater Model Update and Transport Simulations).

**[5.2 Pump-and-Treat Extraction System]{.underline}**

The OU-3 remedial action includes a groundwater pump-and-treat extraction system designed to achieve hydraulic containment of the contaminant plume at its leading edge and to recover contaminated groundwater for treatment. The extraction system is the primary mechanism for preventing further plume migration toward the Ashford County public water supply wellfield and Millhaven Creek.

The extraction system consists of 10 extraction wells installed along a 2,000-foot alignment oriented perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow at the leading edge of the plume. The extraction well alignment is depicted on Figure 5-1 (Appendix B). The extraction wells will be installed at depths of approximately 30 to 45 feet bgs, with screen intervals spanning the full saturated thickness of the overburden aquifer.

**Table 5-1: OU-3 Extraction and ERD System Parameters**

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Parameter**                         **Value**
  ------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Number of Extraction Wells            10

  Extraction Well Alignment Length      2,000 feet

  Anticipated Pumping Rate (per well)   10--25 gpm

  Total Combined Extraction Rate        100--250 gpm

  ERD Injection Points                  36

  ERD Injection Point Spacing           40 feet on center
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------

Each extraction well will be equipped with a submersible pump, level transducer, and flow meter for continuous monitoring and control. Individual well pumping rates are anticipated to range from 10 to 25 gallons per minute (gpm), with a total combined extraction rate of approximately 100 to 250 gpm depending on aquifer response and optimization during the initial operational period. The extraction wells will be connected via a subsurface conveyance header system to the on-site groundwater treatment plant (Section 7).

Capture zone analysis has been performed using the updated groundwater flow model (Appendix I) to verify that the 10-well extraction system will achieve complete capture of the dissolved-phase plume at the leading edge. The model simulations demonstrate that under the design pumping rates, the capture zone extends across the full width of the plume and provides a factor of safety against plume bypass. Optimization of individual well pumping rates will be conducted during the initial 6 months of operation based on observed water levels and capture zone verification monitoring.

The extraction system will be operated continuously following commissioning. Extracted groundwater will be conveyed to the on-site groundwater treatment plant via the subsurface header system and above-grade piping. The treatment plant design is described in Section 7.

**[5.3 In-Situ Enhanced Reductive Dechlorination]{.underline}**

In addition to the pump-and-treat extraction system at the leading edge of the plume, the OU-3 remedial action includes in-situ enhanced reductive dechlorination (ERD) in the mid-plume area to address dissolved-phase chlorinated ethene contamination. ERD is a bioremediation technology that stimulates the activity of indigenous dechlorinating microorganisms (principally *Dehalococcoides* spp.) through the injection of an organic carbon substrate, creating anaerobic conditions that promote sequential reductive dechlorination of TCE and PCE to non-toxic end products (ethene and ethane).

The ERD substrate will consist of emulsified vegetable oil (EVO), which provides a slow-release source of dissolved organic carbon to sustain anaerobic conditions over an extended period. The EVO substrate will be injected through a grid of 36 injection points installed across the mid-plume treatment zone. The injection points will be arranged on 40-foot centers in a grid pattern oriented to provide coverage across the width and length of the mid-plume area, as depicted on Figure 5-2 (Appendix B). Updated groundwater modeling conducted in 2024 (Appendix I) indicates that a 40-foot injection point spacing will achieve adequate substrate distribution within the treatment zone, enabling effective reductive dechlorination across the mid-plume area.

Each injection point will be a direct-push installed well point screened across the primary contaminated interval (approximately 10 to 30 feet bgs). The EVO substrate will be injected using positive-displacement pumps at a target volume of approximately 200 to 400 gallons per injection point, depending on aquifer permeability and acceptance rates at each location. A chase water flush will be applied following EVO injection to distribute the substrate radially from each injection point.

The initial EVO injection event will be performed during the first year of remedy operation. Subsequent reinjection events will be performed on an approximate 18-month cycle, or as indicated by geochemical monitoring data, for the duration of the ERD program. The need for additional injection events will be evaluated based on performance monitoring data, including dissolved oxygen concentrations, oxidation-reduction potential (ORP), ethene and ethane concentrations, and the presence and concentrations of dechlorination daughter products (cis-1,2-DCE, vinyl chloride).

Performance monitoring for the ERD program will be conducted at designated monitoring wells within and downgradient of the ERD treatment zone. Monitoring parameters will include VOCs, dissolved gases (methane, ethene, ethane), geochemical indicators (dissolved oxygen, ORP, pH, specific conductance, ferrous iron, sulfate, nitrate), and microbial assessment (quantitative polymerase chain reaction \[qPCR\] for *Dehalococcoides* spp.).

**[5.4 Groundwater Cleanup Levels and Points of Compliance]{.underline}**

The groundwater cleanup levels applicable to the OU-3 remedial action are those presented in Section 2.2 and Table 2-1 of this RAWP. For clarity, the cleanup levels are reiterated here:

> • TCE: ≤ 5 µg/L
>
> • PCE: ≤ 5 µg/L
>
> • 1,4-Dioxane: ≤ 3.5 µg/L, consistent with Ohio EPA\'s established groundwater quality standard for 1,4-dioxane
>
> • Hexavalent Chromium: ≤ 100 µg/L

The points of compliance for the groundwater remedy are the designated point-of-compliance monitoring wells installed along the Site boundary, as depicted on Figure 5-3. These wells are positioned to monitor groundwater quality at the property boundary and downgradient of the principal remedy components. Compliance with cleanup levels will be assessed through the groundwater monitoring program described in Section 5.5.

Demonstration of cleanup level attainment requires 8 consecutive semi-annual sampling rounds in which all point-of-compliance wells show concentrations at or below the established cleanup levels for all COCs. Upon achieving this demonstration, a request for transition to long-term monitoring or site closeout will be submitted to EPA for review and approval.

**[Section 6 --- OU-4: Riparian Corridor Remedial Action]{.underline}**

**[6.1 Floodplain Soil Excavation]{.underline}**

OU-4 encompasses a 4.5-acre reach of the Millhaven Creek riparian corridor adjacent to the southern boundary of the Site. Historical releases from the Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. facility resulted in contamination of floodplain soils with PCP, metals, and SVOCs at concentrations exceeding ecological risk-based screening levels established during the Baseline Ecological Risk Assessment conducted as part of the RI/FS.

The remedial action for OU-4 consists of excavation of contaminated floodplain soils to a depth of 3 feet bgs within the areas where soil concentrations exceed the ecological risk-based cleanup levels. The 3-foot excavation depth was established in the ROD based on the typical root zone depth and the depth of biological activity for soil-dwelling organisms within the riparian zone.

The estimated excavation volume for OU-4 is 5,900 cubic yards. The excavation footprint has been refined based on the 2024 PDI supplemental soil sampling data, which provided additional spatial resolution of contaminant distribution within the riparian zone. The refined excavation limits are depicted on Figure 6-1 (Appendix B).

Excavation within the riparian corridor will be conducted using a phased approach to minimize disturbance to the stream channel and riparian habitat. Excavation will be performed during low-flow conditions (typically July through October) to reduce the risk of sediment mobilization and transport. The following environmental controls will be implemented during excavation:

> • Silt fencing and sediment barriers installed along the creek bank to prevent sediment discharge to Millhaven Creek.
>
> • Turbidity monitoring in Millhaven Creek upstream and downstream of the work area during active excavation.
>
> • Equipment exclusion zones along the immediate stream bank to prevent bank destabilization.
>
> • Temporary stream diversion, if necessary, for work within the immediate floodplain.

Confirmatory sampling of excavation bottoms will be conducted at 25-foot intervals and analyzed for the ecological risk-based COC list. Excavated soils will be loaded into lined trucks and transported to Northland Disposal Services, Inc. in Seneca County, Ohio for off-site disposal.

**[6.2 Habitat Restoration]{.underline}**

Following completion of floodplain soil excavation and confirmatory verification, the excavated areas within OU-4 will be restored to support native riparian habitat. Restoration activities will include placement of clean fill and topsoil, establishment of native riparian vegetation, and stabilization of disturbed areas to prevent erosion.

The Habitat Restoration Plan (Appendix K) provides detailed specifications for the restoration program, including:

> • Placement of 12 inches of clean topsoil over the backfilled excavation areas.
>
> • Revegetation with native riparian plant species, including a mix of native grasses, forbs, shrubs, and tree species appropriate for the central Ohio riparian zone. Species selection will emphasize wildlife habitat value, erosion control, and stream bank stabilization.
>
> • Planting densities of approximately 400 stems per acre for tree species and 1,000 stems per acre for shrub species.
>
> • Temporary irrigation during the first growing season to support plant establishment.
>
> • Erosion control blankets on slopes and in areas adjacent to the stream channel.
>
> • Installation of large woody debris structures and root wads along the stream bank to provide aquatic habitat complexity.

The Habitat Restoration Plan has been developed in coordination with the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) and will be submitted for review and approval prior to implementation. Coordination with USFWS will ensure that restoration activities are consistent with federal guidelines for riparian and aquatic habitat restoration in the region and that any threatened or endangered species concerns are appropriately addressed.

**[6.3 Ecological Monitoring Program]{.underline}**

A post-restoration ecological monitoring program will be implemented for a duration of 3 years following the completion of habitat restoration activities at OU-4. The purpose of the monitoring program is to evaluate the success of the habitat restoration in achieving the ecological RAOs established in the ROD and to identify any corrective actions that may be needed to ensure long-term ecological recovery.

The ecological monitoring program will include the following components:

> • **Benthic Macroinvertebrate Surveys:** Annual surveys will be conducted during spring and fall index periods at monitoring stations within the restored reach and at upstream and downstream reference stations. Surveys will follow Ohio EPA biological assessment protocols and will include calculation of community indices such as the Invertebrate Community Index (ICI).
>
> • **Surface Water Quality Monitoring:** Water quality sampling will be conducted quarterly during Year 1 and semi-annually during Years 2 and 3 at locations upstream and downstream of the restored area. Parameters will include field measurements (dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature, conductivity, turbidity) and laboratory analysis for COCs at concentrations relevant to aquatic life protection.
>
> • **Vegetation Survival Assessments:** Annual assessments of planted vegetation survival and growth will be conducted during the growing season (July through September). Assessments will document survival rates, canopy cover, species composition, and evidence of invasive species encroachment. A survival rate threshold of 80 percent for tree and shrub plantings at the end of the 3-year monitoring period will be used as the success criterion.

Success criteria for the ecological monitoring program are defined in the Ecological Monitoring Plan (Appendix L). If success criteria are not met at the end of the 3-year monitoring period, additional corrective planting and/or monitoring may be conducted as determined in consultation with EPA and USFWS.

Annual ecological monitoring reports will be prepared and submitted to EPA within 90 days of the completion of each annual monitoring event.

**[Section 7 --- On-Site Groundwater Treatment Plant Design]{.underline}**

**[7.1 Treatment Train Overview]{.underline}**

An on-site groundwater treatment plant will be constructed to treat extracted groundwater from the OU-3 pump-and-treat extraction system and DNAPL recovery condensate from the OU-1 steam-enhanced extraction (SEE) system. The treatment plant will be located within the central portion of the Site, adjacent to the OU-1 construction staging area, as depicted on Figure 7-1 (Appendix J).

The treatment plant is designed to treat a combined influent flow of up to 300 gallons per minute (gpm), comprising up to 250 gpm from the OU-3 extraction system and up to 50 gpm from the OU-1 SEE system. The treatment train consists of the following unit processes, in sequence:

**1. Equalization and Pre-Treatment.** Influent groundwater and SEE condensate will be received in a 50,000-gallon equalization tank to dampen flow and concentration variations. Pre-treatment will include oil/water separation for removal of free-phase DNAPL and petroleum hydrocarbons, followed by metals precipitation for removal of dissolved hexavalent chromium. Chromium reduction will be achieved by ferrous sulfate addition under acidic conditions (pH 2.5--3.0), followed by neutralization and hydroxide precipitation at pH 8.5--9.0. Precipitated metals sludge will be dewatered using a plate-and-frame filter press and disposed off-site as hazardous waste.

**2. Air Stripping.** Pre-treated water will be pumped to a packed tower air stripper for removal of volatile organic compounds, including TCE, PCE, cis-1,2-DCE, and vinyl chloride. The air stripper will consist of a 4-foot-diameter tower packed with 20 feet of polypropylene packing media, operating at an air-to-water ratio of approximately 80:1. The air stripper is designed to achieve greater than 99 percent removal of TCE and PCE. Off-gas from the air stripper will be treated through a vapor-phase granular activated carbon (GAC) adsorption system prior to atmospheric discharge, in compliance with Ohio EPA air quality requirements.

**3. Granular Activated Carbon (GAC) Polishing.** Air stripper effluent will pass through a two-vessel lead/lag GAC adsorption system for polishing removal of residual VOCs and 1,4-dioxane. Each GAC vessel will contain approximately 20,000 pounds of liquid-phase GAC media. The lead/lag configuration allows for continuous operation during media change-outs; when the lead vessel reaches breakthrough, it is taken off-line for media replacement and the lag vessel becomes the new lead vessel. The GAC polishing step is expected to achieve adequate removal of residual contaminants, including 1,4-dioxane, to meet applicable discharge and cleanup standards. GAC media change-out frequency will be determined based on effluent monitoring results and vendor-estimated carbon usage rates.

The treated water effluent from the GAC polishing system will be discharged to Millhaven Creek under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) permit to be obtained from Ohio EPA. The treatment plant design flow, treatment process specifications, and discharge quality targets are presented in the Treatment Plant Design Drawings and Specifications (Appendix J).

The treatment plant will be housed in a pre-engineered metal building with concrete foundation. Electrical service will be provided via a dedicated utility connection. The plant will be designed for remote monitoring and control capability, with telemetry systems providing real-time monitoring of flow rates, tank levels, and effluent quality parameters to the plant operator.

**[7.2 Discharge and Effluent Monitoring]{.underline}**

Treated groundwater will be discharged to Millhaven Creek under an NPDES permit to be obtained from Ohio EPA prior to the commencement of treatment plant operations. The NPDES permit application will be prepared and submitted during the construction phase, with an anticipated permit issuance prior to system start-up.

Effluent monitoring will be conducted at the treatment plant discharge point prior to release to Millhaven Creek. Monitoring parameters and frequencies will be established in the NPDES permit; anticipated requirements include:

> • Daily monitoring for flow rate, pH, and temperature.
>
> • Weekly monitoring for total suspended solids (TSS) and total VOCs.
>
> • Monthly monitoring for TCE, PCE, vinyl chloride, 1,4-dioxane, hexavalent chromium, and total chromium.
>
> • Quarterly whole effluent toxicity (WET) testing.

Effluent quality limits will be established in the NPDES permit consistent with Ohio water quality standards for the receiving stream (Millhaven Creek). Discharge monitoring reports will be submitted to Ohio EPA on a monthly basis in accordance with the NPDES permit requirements.

**[Section 9 --- Community Air Monitoring Plan]{.underline}**

**[9.1 Overview and Objectives]{.underline}**

The Community Air Monitoring Plan (CAMP) establishes the air monitoring program to be implemented during all intrusive remedial action activities at OU-1, OU-2, and OU-4. The CAMP is designed to protect the health and safety of on-site workers and the surrounding community, including residents of the Millhaven Heights neighborhood, from potential exposure to airborne particulates and volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions generated during excavation, grading, thermal treatment, and other construction activities.

Real-time air monitoring will be conducted at the Site perimeter (fenceline) during all periods of active intrusive work. Monitoring data will be used to assess compliance with action levels and to trigger response actions if exceedances are detected.

**[9.2 Monitoring Parameters and Action Levels]{.underline}**

The CAMP monitoring parameters and associated action levels are presented in Table 9-1.

**Table 9-1: CAMP Action Levels**

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Parameter**                        **Action Level**                **Monitoring Instrument**
  ------------------------------------ ------------------------------- --------------------------------
  PM-10 (Particulate Matter ≤ 10 µm)   150 µg/m³ (15-minute average)   Real-time nephelometer

  Total VOCs                           10 ppmv (15-minute average)     Photoionization detector (PID)
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

PM-10 will be monitored using real-time nephelometers (e.g., TSI DustTrak or equivalent) capable of providing continuous 1-minute average concentrations. The PM-10 action level of 150 µg/m³ is based on the National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS) for PM-10 and is consistent with EPA guidance for community air monitoring at Superfund sites.

Total VOCs will be monitored using photoionization detectors (PIDs) equipped with 10.6 eV lamps, calibrated daily with isobutylene standard gas. The fenceline action level for total VOCs is 10 ppmv, measured as a 15-minute average concentration.

Monitoring locations will be established at a minimum of 4 points around the active work area perimeter, including at least one upwind station and at least two downwind stations oriented toward the nearest sensitive receptors (the Millhaven Heights residential neighborhood to the east). Monitoring station locations may be adjusted based on prevailing wind direction as determined by the on-site meteorological station.

Air monitoring will be conducted continuously during all hours of active intrusive work operations. Data will be logged electronically and reviewed in real-time by the Site Health and Safety Officer.

**[9.3 Response Actions]{.underline}**

If monitoring data indicate an exceedance of either the PM-10 or VOC action level at any fenceline monitoring station, the following response protocol will be implemented:

1\. **Immediate Work Stoppage:** All intrusive work activities within the area potentially contributing to the exceedance will be suspended.

2\. **Source Investigation:** The Site Health and Safety Officer will investigate the source of the exceedance and identify contributing factors.

3\. **Corrective Measures:** Appropriate corrective measures will be implemented, which may include application of dust suppression (water spray, calcium chloride), application of foam suppressant to exposed excavation faces, installation of temporary wind screens, and/or modification of work practices.

4\. **Notification:** If the exceedance is sustained for more than 15 minutes, notification will be provided to the EPA RPM (Dr. Sandra Volkov) and to the community via the notification procedures established in the Community Notification Plan (Appendix H).

5\. **Resumption Criteria:** Work activities will not resume until monitoring data demonstrate that fenceline concentrations have returned to levels below the action levels for a minimum of 15 consecutive minutes.

All exceedance events, response actions, and monitoring data will be documented in daily air monitoring logs and reported in the semi-annual monitoring reports submitted to EPA.

**[Section 10 --- Transportation and Materials Management Plan]{.underline}**

**[10.1 Haul Routes]{.underline}**

Contaminated soils, hazardous waste, and other materials requiring off-site disposal will be transported from the Site to Northland Disposal Services, Inc. (Seneca County, Ohio) and/or other EPA-approved disposal facilities. The designated haul route for all off-site transport is County Road 12 to Interstate 71. County Road 12 provides the most direct access from the Site to the Interstate highway system and minimizes travel distance for transport vehicles.

Haul trucks will exit the Site via the main entrance on Old Mill Road, proceed south on County Road 12 to the Interstate 71 interchange, and continue via the Interstate highway system to the disposal facility. The return route will follow the same path in reverse. The designated haul route is depicted on Figure 10-1 (Appendix B).

Traffic control measures will be implemented along the haul route during periods of active hauling operations. These measures will include flaggers at the Site entrance during truck movements, pilot vehicles for oversized loads where required by Ohio Department of Transportation (ODOT) regulations, and compliance with all applicable ODOT load limits and permitting requirements. Hauling operations will be conducted Monday through Saturday, 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM.

All transport vehicles will be inspected prior to departure from the Site to ensure loads are properly secured and covered, vehicles are free of external contamination (following on-site decontamination procedures), and all required manifests and shipping papers are present and complete.

**[10.2 Materials Handling and Manifesting]{.underline}**

All contaminated soils and hazardous waste materials transported off-site will be manifested in accordance with RCRA hazardous waste transportation requirements (40 CFR 262 and 263) and applicable U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) regulations (49 CFR 171--180). Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifests (EPA Form 8700-22) will be prepared for each shipment.

Trucks will be decontaminated at the on-site decontamination pad prior to departing the Site. The decontamination pad will consist of a lined, bermed area with a wash-down system. Decontamination rinse water will be collected and routed to the on-site groundwater treatment plant for treatment.

Loads will be covered with tarps or rigid covers to prevent release of materials during transport. Maximum load weights will comply with Ohio DOT legal weight limits. A spill prevention and response plan for transport activities is included as part of the Health and Safety Plan (Appendix H). In the event of a spill or release during transport, the transporter will implement the spill response procedures and provide immediate notification to Terraverde, CCH, EPA, and applicable state and local agencies.

**[Section 11 --- Health and Safety]{.underline}**

**[11.1 Health and Safety Plan Summary]{.underline}**

A site-specific Health and Safety Plan (HASP) has been prepared for the remedial action at the Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site in accordance with 29 CFR 1926.65 (OSHA Safety and Health Regulations for Construction). The HASP addresses all on-site remedial action activities, including excavation, construction, treatment system operation, monitoring, and maintenance. The full HASP is provided as Appendix H.

The HASP has been developed based on the results of a comprehensive hazard analysis that identifies the chemical, physical, and biological hazards associated with each remedial action task. Key elements of the HASP include:

> • **Hazard Analysis:** Identification and evaluation of chemical exposure hazards (VOCs, PCP, hexavalent chromium, DNAPL), physical hazards (heavy equipment, excavation, confined spaces, electrical, noise), and biological hazards (insects, heat/cold stress).
>
> • **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE):** PPE requirements for each work zone and task, ranging from Level D (standard construction attire) for low-risk perimeter activities to Level C (air-purifying respirators, chemical-resistant coveralls) for work within contaminated excavations.
>
> • **Exposure Monitoring:** Real-time personal air monitoring for VOCs and particulates during intrusive activities, supplementing the fenceline CAMP monitoring described in Section 9.
>
> • **Emergency Response Procedures:** Procedures for responding to chemical exposures, injuries, fires, spills, and other emergencies, including evacuation routes, assembly points, and emergency contact information.
>
> • **Medical Surveillance:** All site workers performing remedial action activities will be enrolled in a medical surveillance program in accordance with applicable OSHA regulations.

A Site Health and Safety Officer (SHSO) will be designated by Terraverde and will be present on-site during all active remedial action work. The SHSO is responsible for implementation and enforcement of the HASP, monitoring of site conditions, and coordination with the EPA RPM on health and safety matters.

**[11.2 Emergency Response]{.underline}**

An emergency response plan has been integrated into the site-specific HASP (Appendix H). The emergency response plan establishes procedures and responsibilities for responding to emergencies that may arise during remedial action activities.

The nearest hospital with an emergency department is Ashford County Medical Center, located at 500 West Main Street, Millhaven, Ohio, approximately 4.5 miles from the Site. The hospital route has been pre-established and will be posted at the Site entrance and at all work zone check-in points.
