**[12.2 Compliance Approach]{.underline}**

The remedial action design and implementation described in this RAWP have been developed to achieve compliance with all identified ARARs. The compliance approach for each ARAR category is summarized below.

**Chemical-Specific ARARs.** The soil cleanup standards and groundwater cleanup levels presented in Section 2.2 have been established in accordance with the chemical-specific ARARs, including Safe Drinking Water Act MCLs, Ohio groundwater quality standards, and EPA risk-based screening levels. The thermal treatment emission controls and effluent discharge quality targets are designed to comply with applicable air quality standards and surface water quality standards. RCRA land disposal restrictions will be met for all hazardous waste materials prior to land placement or off-site disposal.

**Location-Specific ARARs.** The OU-4 riparian corridor remedial action and habitat restoration have been designed in coordination with USFWS to address applicable location-specific requirements, including the Clean Water Act Section 404, the Endangered Species Act, floodplain management requirements, and wetland protection requirements. A cultural resources survey was conducted during the RI to evaluate compliance with the National Historic Preservation Act Section 106; no significant cultural resources were identified within the Site. The remedial action design incorporates erosion and sediment control measures, stormwater management, and environmental protection measures consistent with the location-specific ARARs.

**Action-Specific ARARs.** The engineered containment cell (Section 4.2) is designed to comply with RCRA landfill design and closure requirements under 40 CFR 264. Worker health and safety will be addressed through the site-specific HASP prepared in accordance with applicable OSHA regulations. Off-site waste transportation will comply with RCRA and DOT requirements. The NPDES permit for treated groundwater discharge will be obtained in compliance with Clean Water Act requirements. ERD substrate injection will be conducted in compliance with Ohio underground injection control requirements. Construction activities will comply with local noise ordinances, stormwater permit requirements, and all other applicable action-specific ARARs.

Compliance with ARARs will be documented through the construction and performance monitoring programs described in Sections 8, 9, and other applicable sections of this RAWP, and through regulatory permit applications and approvals obtained during the implementation period.

**[Section 13 --- Implementation Schedule]{.underline}**

**[13.1 Construction Schedule]{.underline}**

The remedial action will be implemented in four overlapping phases, as depicted on the Gantt chart (Figure 13-1, Appendix B). The phased approach is designed to optimize resource allocation, minimize environmental disruption, and achieve the RAOs within the timeframes established in the ROD.

**Phase 1 --- Mobilization and Infrastructure (Months 1--6):** This phase includes contractor mobilization, establishment of construction staging areas, installation of temporary facilities, utility connections, monitoring and extraction well installation, and construction of the on-site groundwater treatment plant. Well installation will include all OU-3 extraction wells, OU-2 and OU-3 monitoring wells, and SEE well pairs for OU-1. Treatment plant construction will proceed concurrently with well installation.

**Phase 2 --- OU-1 and OU-2 Excavation and Treatment (Months 7--18):** This phase includes contaminated soil excavation at OU-1 and OU-2, operation of the LTTD thermal treatment system, construction of the OU-2 engineered containment cell, and placement of excavated lagoon materials in the cell. SEE system operation at OU-1 will commence during this phase and continue through Month 24. Backfill and grading of OU-1 excavation areas will follow excavation completion.

**Phase 3 --- OU-4 Excavation and Restoration (Months 12--24):** OU-4 floodplain soil excavation will be scheduled during low-flow periods (July--October). Habitat restoration activities, including topsoil placement and revegetation, will follow excavation completion. The ecological monitoring program will commence upon completion of restoration planting.

**Phase 4 --- OU-3 Operations (Months 6--Ongoing):** The OU-3 pump-and-treat system will be commissioned and begin operation following treatment plant completion (approximately Month 6). The ERD injection program will be initiated during the first year of Phase 4 operations. Long-term groundwater monitoring, treatment plant operation, and ERD reinjection events will continue throughout the operational period.

Key milestone dates and critical path items are identified on the Gantt chart (Figure 13-1). Critical path activities include treatment plant construction (governing Phase 4 start-up), containment cell construction (governing waste placement schedule), and the low-flow window for OU-4 excavation (governing Phase 3 timing).

**[13.2 Remedy Operational Period and RAO Timeline]{.underline}**

The soil and source area RAOs for OU-1 and OU-2 are projected to be achieved within 5 years of the initiation of remedial action construction, which is consistent with the performance standards established in the ROD. This projection accounts for the excavation, thermal treatment, DNAPL recovery, and containment activities described in Sections 3 and 4.

The groundwater remedial action for OU-3 will require an extended operational period to achieve the cleanup levels specified in Section 2.2 across the full extent of the plume. Based on the updated groundwater flow and transport model (Appendix I), groundwater remedial action objectives are projected to be achieved within approximately 45 years of full-scale system operation. The model projects that groundwater cleanup levels for all COCs will be attained at all point-of-compliance wells within approximately 45 years of continuous system operation, accounting for natural attenuation processes, source mass reduction from OU-1 and OU-2 remedial actions, pump-and-treat extraction, and ERD treatment within the mid-plume area.

The 45-year projection incorporates the following assumptions and considerations:

> • Full-scale operation of the pump-and-treat extraction system at the design extraction rates.
>
> • Successful DNAPL source mass reduction through the SEE system, reducing dissolved-phase loading to the plume.
>
> • ERD-enhanced biodegradation within the mid-plume area, reducing dissolved-phase concentrations of chlorinated ethenes.
>
> • Natural attenuation processes, including dispersion, dilution, and biodegradation, contributing to concentration reduction in the distal portions of the plume.

The long-term operation and maintenance (O&M) program will include continuous operation of the pump-and-treat system, periodic ERD reinjection events, semi-annual groundwater monitoring, treatment plant maintenance, and containment cell inspection and maintenance. Annual O&M costs are estimated at approximately \$1.8 million per year during the active operational period.

The first Five-Year Review for the Site is due in September 2026, pursuant to CERCLA Section 121(c). Subsequent Five-Year Reviews will be conducted at five-year intervals for the duration of the remedial action. Each Five-Year Review will evaluate the protectiveness of the remedy, assess progress toward RAO attainment, and identify any need for remedy modifications or optimization.

# CONSENT DECREE

# I. BACKGROUND

The United States of America ("United States" or "Plaintiff"), on behalf of the United States Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA"), filed this action against Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc. ("CCH" or "Defendant"), a corporation organized and existing under the laws of the State of Delaware, with its principal place of business and headquarters located at 4100 Lakeridge Parkway, Suite 600, Cleveland, Ohio 44114, pursuant to Sections 106 and 107 of the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980, as amended ("CERCLA"), 42 U.S.C. §§ 9606, 9607. The United States and CCH (collectively, the "Parties") have agreed to resolve certain claims asserted in this action through entry of this Consent Decree, and the Court, having reviewed the terms and provisions of this Consent Decree and the administrative record, makes the following findings and recitals:

WHEREAS, the former Hargrove Industrial Complex (hereinafter referred to as the "Site") is a 62-acre property located at 1500 Old Mill Road, Millhaven, Ashford County, Ohio 44078, situated on the west bank of Millhaven Creek in a mixed industrial and residential area of Ashford County;

WHEREAS, Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. ("Hargrove Chemical") owned and operated a chemical production facility on the Site from approximately 1954 to 2001, during which time Hargrove Chemical manufactured chlorinated solvents, organic intermediates, and wood-treatment chemicals, and conducted various waste management and disposal operations at the facility, including the operation of unlined wastewater lagoons and direct discharge of process wastewaters;

WHEREAS, the Site was proposed for listing on the National Priorities List ("NPL") on March 14, 2016, and was formally listed on the NPL on September 22, 2016, in accordance with the Hazard Ranking System under CERCLA § 105, 42 U.S.C. § 9605;

WHEREAS, CCH is the successor-in-interest to Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Co. through an asset purchase agreement dated June 14, 2008, pursuant to which CCH acquired substantially all of the assets of Hargrove Chemical, including the Site, and expressly assumed environmental liability for the Site under Article 8.3 of said acquisition agreement;

WHEREAS, CCH is a principal responsible party ("PRP") for the release and threatened release of hazardous substances at and from the Site, within the meaning of CERCLA §§ 107(a)(1)-(4), 42 U.S.C. §§ 9607(a)(1)-(4);

WHEREAS, Terraverde Environmental Sciences, LLC ("Terraverde"), an Ohio limited liability company headquartered at 2280 Greenfield Road, Columbus, Ohio 43215, conducted a Remedial Investigation/Feasibility Study ("RI/FS") for the Site under the direction of EPA, which RI/FS was completed and approved by EPA in June 2019;

WHEREAS, the Remedial Investigation ("RI") identified principal contaminants of concern at the Site including trichloroethylene ("TCE"), tetrachloroethylene ("PCE"), pentachlorophenol ("PCP"), hexavalent chromium, benzo(a)pyrene, and 1,4-dioxane, found in soils and groundwater at concentrations significantly exceeding applicable cleanup levels, with maximum detected concentrations of TCE in groundwater at 18,400 µg/L, PCE at 6,200 µg/L, 1,4-dioxane at 280 µg/L, and hexavalent chromium at 4,100 µg/L, and dense non-aqueous phase liquid ("DNAPL") identified at multiple locations in the subsurface;

WHEREAS, the RI identified four operable units at the Site: OU-1 (Former Production Area, encompassing approximately 18 acres in the central portion of the Site); OU-2 (Wastewater Lagoon Area, encompassing approximately 8 acres in the southeastern portion of the Site); OU-3 (Groundwater Plume, extending approximately 1.2 miles in length by 0.4 miles in width from the Site in a generally northwesterly direction along the regional groundwater flow path); and OU-4 (Riparian Corridor, encompassing approximately 4.5 acres along the western bank of Millhaven Creek adjacent to the Site);

WHEREAS, EPA, Region 5, with the concurrence of the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency ("Ohio EPA"), issued a Record of Decision ("ROD") on September 15, 2021, selecting a comprehensive remedy for the Site, which ROD sets forth the selected remedy, Remedial Action Objectives, Performance Standards, cleanup levels, and Applicable or Relevant and Appropriate Requirements ("ARARs") for each Operable Unit;

WHEREAS, the total estimated cost of the selected remedy is Eighty-Nine Million Four Hundred Thousand Dollars (\$89,400,000) in present value, allocated among the Operable Units as follows: OU-1 (Former Production Area): \$31,200,000; OU-2 (Wastewater Lagoon Area): \$18,700,000; OU-3 (Groundwater Plume): \$28,900,000; and OU-4 (Riparian Corridor): \$10,600,000;

WHEREAS, the Ashford County public water supply wellfield, which serves as the sole source of drinking water for approximately 14,000 residents of the Millhaven and greater Ashford County communities, is located approximately 1.8 miles downgradient of the leading edge of the OU-3 groundwater plume, making timely and effective remediation of the groundwater plume critical to the protection of public health;

WHEREAS, the Millhaven Community Advisory Group ("CAG"), chaired by Ellen Dorsey, participated actively in the ROD public comment process, submitted written comments during the public comment period from May 15, 2021 through July 15, 2021, and attended the public meeting held on June 10, 2021 at the Millhaven Community Center, and the ROD Responsiveness Summary addresses the CAG's comments;

WHEREAS, Ohio EPA's State Project Coordinator Raymond Hess and EPA Region 5 Remedial Project Manager Dr. Sandra Volkov have coordinated oversight of remedial planning activities at the Site and concur with the terms of this Consent Decree;

WHEREAS, the Parties agree, and the Court finds, that this Consent Decree is fair, reasonable, consistent with CERCLA and the NCP, and in the public interest, and that entry of this Consent Decree without further litigation is an appropriate exercise of the Parties' discretion;

WHEREAS, Defendant CCH does not admit any liability to the United States arising out of the transactions or occurrences alleged in the Complaint, but consents to the entry of this Consent Decree and to the jurisdiction of this Court for the purpose of resolving the claims of the United States without litigation;

NOW, THEREFORE, it is hereby ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND DECREED as follows:

## C. Remedial Action Components by Operable Unit

22. **OU-1 (Former Production Area).** Defendant shall perform the following remedial activities at OU-1, in accordance with the ROD and the approved RAWP:

<!-- -->

(a) *Excavation.* Defendant shall excavate contaminated soils exceeding industrial Preliminary Remediation Goals ("PRGs") to a depth of fifteen (15) feet below ground surface ("bgs"), with an estimated excavation volume of forty-two thousand (42,000) cubic yards. Excavation limits shall be determined based on the RI soil sampling data and confirmed through verification sampling in accordance with the approved RAWP.

(b) *DNAPL Recovery.* Defendant shall install and operate a steam-enhanced extraction ("SEE") system for the recovery of dense non-aqueous phase liquid ("DNAPL") from the subsurface, utilizing fourteen (14) injection/extraction well pairs installed at locations and depths specified in the approved RAWP. The SEE system shall be operated until DNAPL recovery rates demonstrate asymptotic conditions, as determined by EPA.

(c) *Ex-Situ Thermal Desorption.* Defendant shall treat all excavated soils from OU-1 by ex-situ thermal desorption to a treatment standard of one milligram per kilogram (1 mg/kg) total volatile organic compounds ("VOCs"). Treated soils meeting the treatment standard shall be verified through confirmation sampling at a frequency of no less than one sample per five hundred (500) cubic yards.

(d) *Backfill and Disposal.* Treated soils meeting the 1 mg/kg total VOC treatment standard may be used as backfill material at the Site. Soils that do not meet the treatment standard after thermal desorption shall be disposed of off-site at a facility permitted under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act ("RCRA"), Subtitle C.

(e) *Institutional Controls.* Defendant shall implement and maintain institutional controls restricting land use at OU-1 to industrial and commercial uses only, in the form of environmental covenants recorded in the Ashford County land records in accordance with the Ohio Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, Ohio Rev. Code §§ 5301.80-5301.92.

<!-- -->

23. **OU-2 (Wastewater Lagoon Area).** Defendant shall perform the following remedial activities at OU-2, in accordance with the ROD and the approved RAWP:

<!-- -->

(a) *Excavation.* Defendant shall excavate lagoon sediments and underlying contaminated soils to the native clay confining layer, located at approximately twelve (12) feet below ground surface, with an estimated excavation volume of twenty-eight thousand five hundred (28,500) cubic yards.

(b) *On-Site Consolidation.* Defendant shall consolidate excavated materials in an on-site engineered containment cell constructed with a composite liner system consisting of a sixty-mil (60-mil) high-density polyethylene ("HDPE") geomembrane overlying a minimum of twenty-four inches (24 inches) of compacted clay with a maximum hydraulic conductivity of 1 × 10⁻⁷ cm/sec. The containment cell shall be capped with a RCRA-equivalent cap meeting the requirements of 40 C.F.R. § 264.310, including a composite barrier layer, drainage layer, protective soil cover, and vegetative cover.

(c) *Leachate Collection.* Defendant shall install and maintain a leachate collection and removal system ("LCRS") within the containment cell. Collected leachate shall be conveyed to the on-site groundwater treatment plant for treatment prior to discharge.

(d) *Long-Term Groundwater Monitoring.* Defendant shall install and maintain a minimum of eight (8) downgradient monitoring wells around the containment cell perimeter. Groundwater monitoring shall be conducted quarterly for the first five (5) years following completion of containment cell construction, and semi-annually thereafter, for all contaminants of concern.

<!-- -->

24. **OU-3 (Groundwater Plume).** Defendant shall perform the following remedial activities at OU-3, in accordance with the ROD and the approved RAWP:

<!-- -->

(a) *Pump-and-Treat System.* Defendant shall install and operate a pump-and-treat system consisting of twelve (12) extraction wells installed along a 2,400-foot extraction trench oriented perpendicular to the direction of groundwater flow. The extraction system shall be designed to achieve hydraulic capture of the entire dissolved-phase plume, as demonstrated through capture zone analysis and confirmed through monitoring data.

(b) *Groundwater Treatment Plant.* Defendant shall design, construct, and operate an on-site groundwater treatment plant incorporating the following treatment train: (i) air stripping for removal of volatile organic compounds, with a minimum removal efficiency of 99% for TCE and PCE; (ii) granular activated carbon ("GAC") polishing for residual VOC removal; and (iii) an advanced oxidation process ("AOP") utilizing ultraviolet light/hydrogen peroxide (UV/H₂O₂) for the destruction of 1,4-dioxane, designed to achieve the 0.35 µg/L cleanup level in treated effluent.

(c) *Treated Water Discharge.* Treated water from the groundwater treatment plant shall be discharged to Millhaven Creek under a National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System ("NPDES") permit issued by Ohio EPA, or to another approved discharge point. Defendant shall obtain the NPDES permit prior to commencement of treated water discharge.

(d) *In-Situ Enhanced Reductive Dechlorination.* Defendant shall implement an in-situ enhanced reductive dechlorination ("ERD") program utilizing emulsified vegetable oil ("EVO") substrate injection through a minimum of forty-eight (48) injection points installed at thirty-foot (30-foot) spacing across the mid-plume treatment zone, as delineated in the ROD. ERD injections shall be conducted in a minimum of three (3) annual rounds, with additional rounds as necessary to achieve cleanup levels.

(e) *Groundwater Cleanup Levels.* The Remedial Action for OU-3 shall achieve the following groundwater cleanup levels at the designated point of compliance wells: TCE at or below 5 µg/L; PCE at or below 5 µg/L; 1,4-Dioxane at or below 0.35 µg/L; and Hexavalent Chromium at or below 100 µg/L.

(f) *Monitoring Well Network.* Defendant shall install and maintain a monitoring well network consisting of no fewer than thirty-six (36) wells located throughout the plume area, including sentinel wells, plume-core wells, plume-fringe wells, and point of compliance wells. Groundwater monitoring shall be conducted quarterly for the first three (3) years following startup of the pump-and-treat system, and semi-annually thereafter, until groundwater cleanup levels have been achieved and maintained for eight (8) consecutive semi-annual monitoring rounds.

<!-- -->

25. **OU-4 (Riparian Corridor).** Defendant shall perform the following remedial activities at OU-4, in accordance with the ROD and the approved RAWP:

<!-- -->

(a) *Excavation.* Defendant shall excavate contaminated floodplain soils to a depth of three (3) feet below ground surface across the 4.5-acre OU-4 area, with an estimated excavation volume of six thousand eight hundred (6,800) cubic yards. Excavated materials shall be consolidated in the OU-2 containment cell or disposed of off-site at a RCRA-permitted facility.

(b) *Restoration.* Following excavation, Defendant shall restore the OU-4 area with clean fill material meeting background soil quality standards, topsoil, and native riparian vegetation in accordance with a Habitat Restoration Plan prepared in consultation with and approved by both the United States Fish and Wildlife Service ("USFWS") and the Ohio Department of Natural Resources ("ODNR").

(c) *Ecological Monitoring.* Defendant shall conduct a five-year (5-year) ecological monitoring program following completion of the OU-4 restoration, including: (i) annual benthic macroinvertebrate surveys in Millhaven Creek adjacent to the OU-4 area; (ii) quarterly surface water quality monitoring for contaminants of concern at three upstream and three downstream sampling locations; and (iii) annual vegetation survival and establishment assessments to evaluate the success of riparian revegetation efforts. Monitoring results shall be reported to EPA, USFWS, and ODNR annually.

## D. Cross-Cutting Requirements

26. **Community Air Monitoring.** Defendant shall prepare and implement a Community Air Monitoring Plan ("CAMP") during all intrusive activities at the Site, including excavation, soil handling, thermal desorption operations, and any other activities that may generate airborne contaminants. The CAMP shall include continuous perimeter monitoring for particulate matter (PM-10) and total volatile organic compounds (VOCs) at a minimum of four (4) fenceline monitoring stations. Action levels shall be established at 150 µg/m³ for PM-10 and 5 parts per million by volume (ppmv) for total VOCs at the fenceline. Exceedance of action levels shall trigger work stoppage and implementation of corrective measures, including dust suppression and enhanced vapor controls, until concentrations return below action levels. The CAMP shall be consistent with the New York State Department of Health Community Air Monitoring Plan guidance, as referenced in the ROD.

27. **Transportation.** All contaminated materials transported from the Site, whether for off-site disposal or for transfer to the on-site treatment area, shall be transported via State Route 47 to Interstate 71, in accordance with the transportation route specified in the ROD. Transport vehicles shall avoid residential areas, including the Millhaven Heights residential subdivision located approximately 0.5 miles east of the Site. All transportation of hazardous waste shall comply with applicable U.S. Department of Transportation regulations at 49 C.F.R. Parts 171-180 and Ohio Department of Transportation requirements.

28. **Health and Safety.** Defendant shall prepare and implement a Health and Safety Plan ("HASP") that is compliant with 29 C.F.R. § 1910.120, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration ("OSHA") Hazardous Waste Operations and Emergency Response ("HAZWOPER") standard. The HASP shall address all anticipated site hazards, personal protective equipment requirements, decontamination procedures, medical surveillance, emergency response procedures, and site control measures. The HASP shall be available for review by EPA and Ohio EPA at all times during performance of the Work.

29. **ARARs Compliance.** Defendant shall comply with all forty-seven (47) federal and state Applicable or Relevant and Appropriate Requirements identified in the ROD's ARARs compliance matrix. The RAWP shall include a detailed ARARs compliance demonstration for each ARAR, describing how the proposed remedy design satisfies each requirement. Defendant shall promptly notify EPA of any circumstances that may affect its ability to comply with any ARAR.

30. **Performance Timeline.** The remedy shall be designed and implemented to achieve Remedial Action Objectives within thirty (30) years for groundwater (OU-3) and within five (5) years of the commencement of remedial construction for soil and source areas (OU-1, OU-2, and OU-4). These timeframes are Performance Standards under this Consent Decree and are subject to the stipulated penalty provisions of Section X.

31. **Five-Year Reviews.** In accordance with CERCLA § 121(c), 42 U.S.C. § 9621(c), Five-Year Reviews of the remedy shall be conducted on a five-year cycle for the duration of the remedial action period. The first Five-Year Review shall be due no later than September 2026. Defendant shall cooperate with EPA in the conduct of each Five-Year Review and shall provide all data, records, and information requested by EPA. Five-Year Reviews shall assess whether the remedy is, or is expected to be, protective of human health and the environment.

# VII. MODIFICATION OF THE ROD / ESD AND ROD AMENDMENT PROCESS

## A. Categories of Modifications

32. The Parties recognize that modifications to the remedy selected in the ROD may be necessary or appropriate during the course of the Remedial Action. Any such modification shall be categorized and processed in accordance with the following framework:

<!-- -->

(a) **Minor Modifications.** Changes to operational details of the remedy that do not alter the scope, Performance Standards, or protectiveness of the remedy may be approved by EPA in writing without an ESD or ROD Amendment. Examples of Minor Modifications include, without limitation: adjustments to construction sequencing that do not affect the overall remediation timeline; minor equipment substitutions of equivalent capacity, function, and performance; relocation of individual monitoring wells by distances of less than fifty (50) feet, provided that the overall spatial coverage of the monitoring network is not diminished; and changes to sampling analytical methods that are of equivalent or greater sensitivity. Minor Modifications shall be documented in writing and maintained in the administrative record.

(b) **Significant Differences (Requiring ESD).** Changes that significantly alter but do not fundamentally change the remedy selected in the ROD require an Explanation of Significant Differences under CERCLA § 117(c), 42 U.S.C. § 9617(c), and 40 C.F.R. § 300.435(c)(2)(i). Examples of changes that may constitute significant differences include, without limitation: changes to excavation depths or excavation volumes that reduce the scope of source removal by more than ten percent (10%); changes to treatment standards that relax performance criteria for any treatment technology specified in the ROD; reductions in the number of extraction wells, injection wells, or monitoring wells that may affect system performance or monitoring coverage; changes to monitoring programs that reduce sampling frequency or spatial coverage below the minimums specified in the ROD; and modifications to containment cell design specifications that reduce the level of protectiveness.

(c) **Fundamental Changes (Requiring ROD Amendment).** Changes that fundamentally alter the remedy selected in the ROD require a ROD Amendment under 40 C.F.R. § 300.435(c)(2)(ii), including public notice and an opportunity for public comment. Examples of changes that constitute fundamental changes include, without limitation: changes to cleanup levels for any contaminant of concern; elimination of a treatment technology component specified in the ROD, including but not limited to the elimination of advanced oxidation processes, thermal desorption, air stripping, or in-situ treatment technologies; substitution of a fundamentally different remedial approach for any Operable Unit; and changes that would result in the remedy failing to meet Remedial Action Objectives within the timeframe specified in the ROD.

<!-- -->

33. The distinction between changes requiring an ESD and those requiring a ROD Amendment shall be determined by EPA in its sole discretion. Defendant may request a determination from EPA regarding the appropriate category for a proposed modification, but Defendant shall not implement any change requiring an ESD or ROD Amendment until the applicable process has been completed and EPA has issued the ESD or ROD Amendment. Implementation of a modification requiring an ESD or ROD Amendment without completion of the applicable process shall constitute a violation of this Consent Decree.

## B. Procedure for Requesting Modifications

# X. STIPULATED PENALTIES

## A. Applicability

48. Defendant shall be liable for stipulated penalties to the United States for failure to comply with the requirements of this Consent Decree as set forth in this Section. Stipulated penalties shall begin to accrue on the day a violation occurs and shall continue to accrue through the date on which compliance is achieved or the violation is cured, as determined by EPA. Stipulated penalties are in addition to, and do not limit, any other remedies, sanctions, or penalties available to the United States under CERCLA, RCRA, or any other applicable federal or state law. Payment of stipulated penalties shall not excuse Defendant from performing any Work required under this Consent Decree, nor shall payment of stipulated penalties constitute a waiver of any rights of the United States under this Consent Decree or applicable law.

## B. Penalty Schedule for Major Deviations

49. Defendant shall pay stipulated penalties in the amount of **Five Thousand Dollars (\$5,000) per day** for each day of noncompliance for each "Major Deviation" from the requirements of this Consent Decree. A "Major Deviation" is defined as:

<!-- -->

(i) Failure to achieve Performance Standards set forth in the ROD, including but not limited to cleanup levels, treatment standards, and Remedial Action Objective timeframes;

(ii) Failure to implement a remedial technology or component required by the ROD, including but not limited to omission of a treatment unit, failure to install the specified number of extraction wells, injection wells, or monitoring wells, or failure to construct remedy components to the design specifications set forth in the ROD;

(iii) Construction or operation of remedy components that do not meet ROD design specifications, including but not limited to containment cell liner thickness, excavation depths, treatment system capacity, and extraction system configuration;

(iv) Failure to comply with cleanup levels or treatment standards specified in the ROD at any Operable Unit;

(v) Failure to achieve groundwater Remedial Action Objectives within the timeframe specified in the ROD, including the thirty-year (30-year) timeframe for groundwater cleanup and the five-year (5-year) timeframe for soil and source area remediation; and

(vi) Implementation of modifications to the ROD remedy without prior EPA approval through the applicable ESD or ROD Amendment process set forth in Section VII of this Consent Decree.

<!-- -->

50. For Major Deviations involving ongoing design or operational deficiencies, including but not limited to a treatment system that does not include a required technology component, a containment cell constructed with a liner system that does not meet ROD specifications, or an extraction system with fewer wells than specified in the ROD, stipulated penalties shall accrue from the date the deficient system or component becomes operational and shall continue to accrue until the deficiency is corrected to EPA's satisfaction.

## C. Penalty Schedule for Minor Deviations

51. Defendant shall pay stipulated penalties in the amount of **One Thousand Five Hundred Dollars (\$1,500) per day** for each day of noncompliance for each "Minor Deviation" from the requirements of this Consent Decree. A "Minor Deviation" is defined as:

<!-- -->

(i) Late submission of any deliverable required under this Consent Decree, including the RAWP, progress reports, monitoring data, and annual status reports;

(ii) Failure to comply with administrative or procedural requirements of this Consent Decree, including but not limited to incorrect regulatory citations in plans or reports, incomplete ARARs compliance matrices, or failure to include required certifications;

(iii) Deviations from the transportation routes specified in the ROD and Section VI.D of this Consent Decree;

(iv) Failure to maintain the specified number of monitoring wells or the specified monitoring frequency at any Operable Unit, where the deviation does not directly result in failure to detect contamination migration or failure to evaluate remedy performance;

(v) Deficiencies in the Health and Safety Plan, Community Air Monitoring Plan, or other ancillary plans that are inconsistent with the specifications set forth in the ROD or this Consent Decree but do not directly affect the protectiveness of the remedy.

<!-- -->

52. EPA reserves the right to reclassify a Minor Deviation as a Major Deviation if, in EPA's judgment, the deviation compromises or has the potential to compromise the protectiveness of the remedy or the protection of human health and the environment. EPA shall notify Defendant in writing of any reclassification, and the Major Deviation penalty rate shall apply from the date of the reclassification forward.

## D. Penalty Payment and Procedures

53. EPA shall notify Defendant in writing of any stipulated penalty demand, specifying the nature of the violation, the applicable penalty rate, the period of noncompliance, and the total penalty amount demanded.

54. Defendant shall pay stipulated penalties within thirty (30) days of receipt of EPA's demand. # XII. FORCE MAJEURE

67. Defendant shall not be liable for stipulated penalties for delays in performance of the Work that are caused by events constituting Force Majeure. Force Majeure events may include, without limitation: acts of God, such as floods, earthquakes, hurricanes, and tornadoes; war or armed conflict; national emergencies; labor disputes not involving Defendant's employees or Defendant's contractors' employees; fire; epidemics or pandemics; and any orders of governmental authorities issued in response to such events.

68. Force Majeure does not include, and Defendant shall not assert as Force Majeure: increased costs of performance; changed financial conditions of Defendant, including bankruptcy or insolvency; normal weather conditions for the geographic area; failure of Defendant's contractors or subcontractors to perform their obligations, unless such failure is itself caused by a Force Majeure event; or regulatory changes that were foreseeable at the time of entry of this Consent Decree.

70. The burden of demonstrating that an event constitutes Force Majeure and that the delay was caused by such event rests with Defendant. **[1. Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**

The purpose of this memorandum is to summarize the results of the Pre-Design Investigation (PDI) conducted at Operable Unit 1 (OU-1), the Former Production Area, and Operable Unit 2 (OU-2), the Wastewater Lagoon Area, of the Former Hargrove Industrial Complex Superfund Site located at 1500 Old Mill Road, Millhaven, Ashford County, Ohio 44078 (the \"Site\"). The PDI was performed by Terraverde Environmental Sciences, LLC (\"Terraverde\") on behalf of Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc. (\"CCH\") to refine the conceptual site model and generate the data necessary to support the development of the Remedial Action Work Plan (RAWP) for the selected remedy at OU-1 and OU-2.

The PDI was conducted in accordance with the Record of Decision (ROD) issued September 15, 2021, by the United States Environmental Protection Agency, Region 5. The EPA Remedial Project Manager for the Site is Dr. Sandra Volkov. The State of Ohio Environmental Protection Agency concurred in the ROD; the State Project Coordinator is Raymond Hess. The ROD selected a comprehensive remedy for both operable units, including soil excavation, steam-enhanced extraction (SEE) of dense non-aqueous phase liquid (DNAPL) source material, thermal desorption treatment, and containment cell construction at OU-2, among other components.

CCH is the responsible party obligated to implement the selected remedy pursuant to a Consent Decree entered by the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio on March 12, 2020, in the matter of *United States v. Cascade Chemical Holdings, Inc.*, Case No. 3:20-cv-00487-JHR. The Consent Decree requires CCH to implement the remedy \"in accordance with\" the ROD, the Statement of Work attached thereto, and all applicable guidance and regulations.

This PDI builds upon the Remedial Investigation / Feasibility Study (RI/FS) completed by Terraverde in 2019, which characterized site-wide contamination, evaluated remedial alternatives, and provided the technical basis for the ROD. The Site is a 62-acre former chemical manufacturing facility listed on the National Priorities List (NPL) on September 22, 2016. The former Hargrove Chemical Manufacturing Company operated at the Site from 1954 to 2001, producing organic solvents, wood preservatives, and specialty chemical compounds. CCH acquired the Hargrove assets through a corporate acquisition in 2008.

PDI fieldwork was conducted between June 3 and September 20, 2024. All soil, groundwater, and DNAPL samples collected during the PDI were submitted for laboratory analysis to Clearwater Analytical Laboratories, Inc. (\"Clearwater\"), located in Columbus, Ohio. Clearwater is accredited by the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency, Bureau of Environmental Health, and maintains current NELAP accreditation.

The findings presented herein will directly inform the forthcoming RAWP, which is targeted for submission to EPA Region 5 by January 2025. Terraverde anticipates preparing a draft RAWP for CCH internal review by December 2024 prior to formal submission.

**[2. PDI Scope and Methodology]{.underline}**

**[2.1 OU-1 --- Former Production Area (18 Acres)]{.underline}**

The PDI scope for OU-1 encompassed the advancement of twelve (12) soil borings, designated PDI-SB-01 through PDI-SB-12, across the 18-acre Former Production Area. The primary objectives of the OU-1 PDI were to: (1) refine the vertical and lateral extent of soil contamination within the production area footprint; (2) delineate the DNAPL source zone identified during the RI; and (3) generate design-level data to support excavation depth determination and SEE system design for the RAWP.

Borings were advanced to a maximum depth of 20 feet below ground surface (bgs) using a combination of direct-push technology (Geoprobe Model 7822DT) and hollow-stem auger (HSA) methods. Direct-push methods were employed at locations where subsurface conditions permitted continuous advancement to target depth. HSA drilling was utilized at locations where cobble fill or refusal conditions prevented direct-push advancement. All borings were continuously sampled at 2-foot intervals from ground surface to total depth, yielding a comprehensive vertical profile of contamination at each location.

Soil samples were submitted to Clearwater Analytical Laboratories for analysis of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) by EPA Method 8260C, semi-volatile organic compounds (SVOCs) by EPA Method 8270E, total chromium by EPA Method 6010D, and hexavalent chromium by EPA Method 7196A. These analytes constitute the primary contaminants of concern (COCs) identified in the RI/FS and designated in the ROD.

Field screening was performed on all soil samples using a MiniRAE 3000 photoionization detector (PID) equipped with a 10.6 eV lamp. PID readings were recorded in the field logs and used for real-time screening of soil conditions during boring advancement.

In addition to the soil borings, Terraverde conducted a DNAPL investigation program consisting of interface probe measurements in existing site monitoring wells (MW-4, MW-7, MW-9, and MW-11) and in six (6) newly installed temporary well points (TW-01 through TW-06) to assess the presence and apparent thickness of DNAPL within the suspected source zone. The temporary well points were installed using direct-push methods and screened across the water table interface.

Furthermore, pilot-scale steam injection testing was conducted at two locations within the DNAPL source zone to evaluate steam distribution radius and extraction efficiency as design parameters for the full-scale SEE system specified in the ROD. Each pilot test utilized a single injection well / extraction well pair to assess thermal propagation under site-specific geologic conditions. The results of this testing are presented in Section 3.3.

**[2.2 OU-2 --- Wastewater Lagoon Area (8 Acres)]{.underline}**

The PDI scope for OU-2 encompassed the advancement of nine (9) soil borings, designated PDI-LG-01 through PDI-LG-09, across the three former unlined wastewater lagoon areas (Lagoons 1, 2, and 3) that comprise the 8-acre OU-2 footprint. The primary objectives of the OU-2 PDI were to: (1) characterize the depth and concentration of residual contamination within the lagoon soils; (2) delineate the vertical position and lateral continuity of the native clay confining layer that forms the natural base of the contaminated zone; and (3) generate geotechnical data to support the design of the containment cell specified in the ROD.

Borings were advanced to a maximum depth of 18 feet bgs using hollow-stem auger methods. Continuous soil sampling was performed at 2-foot intervals from ground surface to total depth. Soil samples were submitted to Clearwater Analytical Laboratories for analysis of pentachlorophenol (PCP) by EPA Method 8270E, total chromium by EPA Method 6010D, hexavalent chromium by EPA Method 7196A, SVOCs by EPA Method 8270E, and benzo(a)pyrene by EPA Method 8270E. These analytes represent the principal COCs identified in the OU-2 RI characterization.

A geotechnical evaluation of subsurface materials was conducted in coordination with Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants, LLC (\"Pinnacle\"), of Cleveland, Ohio. Pinnacle collected undisturbed Shelby tube samples from representative borings within the lagoon footprint for laboratory analysis of soil strength, compressibility, and permeability parameters necessary for containment cell foundation design. Pinnacle also performed visual classification and Unified Soil Classification System (USCS) logging of all OU-2 borings.

Permeability testing was performed in four (4) temporary well points (TW-07 through TW-10) installed within the lagoon footprint using rising-head and falling-head slug test methods. These tests were designed to characterize the hydraulic conductivity of the native clay layer and overlying fill materials for use in groundwater modeling and containment cell design calculations.

**[2.3 Quality Assurance / Quality Control]{.underline}**

Field QA/QC measures were implemented throughout the PDI in accordance with the approved Sampling and Analysis Plan (SAP) and Quality Assurance Project Plan (QAPP). Field duplicate samples were collected at a rate of one (1) per ten (10) investigative samples. Equipment rinsate blanks were collected daily for non-dedicated sampling equipment. Trip blanks accompanied all VOC sample shipments from the field to the laboratory.

Laboratory QA/QC was performed by Clearwater Analytical Laboratories in accordance with Clearwater\'s internal QAPP and the project-specific QAPP. Method blanks, laboratory control samples, matrix spikes, and matrix spike duplicates were analyzed with each analytical batch. All analytical data generated during the PDI underwent Terraverde Level III data validation in accordance with EPA Region 5 data validation guidelines. Overall data quality was rated as \"usable without qualification\" for approximately 94% of the analytical results. The remaining 6% of results were qualified as estimated (\"J\" flagged) due to minor holding time exceedances for select SVOC samples collected during the final week of field operations. These qualified results are considered usable for site characterization and design purposes.

**[3. OU-1 PDI Results --- Former Production Area]{.underline}**

**[3.1 Soil Contamination --- Vertical Extent]{.underline}**

The twelve OU-1 soil borings (PDI-SB-01 through PDI-SB-12) were evaluated to determine the vertical extent of contamination relative to the industrial-use Preliminary Remediation Goals (PRGs) established in the ROD. The complete analytical results are provided in Attachment A. A summary of the findings is presented below.

Seven of the twelve borings (PDI-SB-01, -02, -04, -05, -07, -09, and -11) showed contamination defined as COC concentrations exceeding industrial PRGs terminating above 12 feet bgs. In these borings, the deepest exceedance was observed between 8 and 11.5 feet bgs. Below these depths, COC concentrations were either non-detect or below applicable PRGs. The majority of borings therefore indicate that contamination is confined to the upper 12 feet of the soil column in the western and northern portions of OU-1.

However, five of the twelve borings (PDI-SB-03, -06, -08, -10, and -12) detected contamination at concentrations exceeding industrial PRGs at depths at or below 15 feet bgs. These five borings are concentrated in the central and eastern portions of OU-1, in the vicinity of the former reactor building and chemical storage area --- areas historically associated with the most intensive manufacturing operations and identified in the RI as the probable DNAPL source zone. The specific exceedances at depth are summarized below:

Of particular note, the hexavalent chromium concentration at PDI-SB-08 at 13.5 feet bgs was 42 mg/kg, nearly seven times the industrial PRG of 6.3 mg/kg. Similarly, TCE concentrations at PDI-SB-12 at 15 feet bgs were 18 mg/kg, more than five times the PRG. These concentrations represent substantial exceedances that cannot be attributed to minor residual impacts and are consistent with active contaminant migration to depth in the DNAPL source area.

The spatial distribution of the deeper contamination is significant. All five borings with exceedances at or below 15 feet bgs are located within or immediately adjacent to the central and eastern portions of OU-1, covering an area of approximately 7 to 8 acres. These borings cluster around the former reactor building foundation and the drum storage pad area, where historical operations involved the handling, processing, and temporary storage of concentrated solvent waste streams and wood-treating solutions.

In summary, while the majority of borings (7 of 12) indicate contamination is confined to the upper 12 feet, the remaining borings (5 of 12) demonstrate that contamination extends to 13.5 to 15.0 feet bgs in the central and eastern portions of OU-1. Additional delineation may be warranted in the central and eastern portions of OU-1 to ensure complete source removal in those areas. The implications of these findings for excavation depth determination are discussed further in Sections 3.4 and 5.1.

**[3.2 DNAPL Source Zone Characterization]{.underline}**

DNAPL was detected as measurable free-phase product in four (4) of the six (6) temporary well points installed during the PDI (TW-01, TW-03, TW-04, and TW-06). Apparent DNAPL thickness ranged from 0.02 feet at TW-06 to 0.18 feet at TW-03. Interface probe measurements in existing monitoring wells confirmed the presence of sheens or trace DNAPL at MW-7 and MW-9, consistent with RI-phase observations. No measurable DNAPL was detected in MW-4 or MW-11, which are located at the periphery of the suspected source area.

The DNAPL source zone is concentrated within the central OU-1 area, extending from the former reactor building eastward to the chemical storage area. Based on the PDI well point and monitoring well data, the lateral extent of the DNAPL source zone is estimated to cover approximately 2.8 acres within the 18-acre OU-1 footprint. This estimate is consistent with the RI-phase delineation but provides improved resolution based on the additional well point data.

Soil concentrations within the DNAPL zone consistently exceed calculated saturation concentrations for TCE and PCP, confirming the presence of residual DNAPL in both the vadose zone and the shallow saturated zone. The DNAPL zone is coincident with the five soil borings (PDI-SB-03, -06, -08, -10, and -12) that exhibit contamination at or below 15 feet bgs, reinforcing the conclusion that deeper contamination in the central and eastern portions of OU-1 is associated with DNAPL migration and underscoring the need for deeper excavation and aggressive source treatment in these areas.

**[3.3 Steam-Enhanced Extraction (SEE) Pilot Test Results]{.underline}**

Two pilot-scale steam injection tests were conducted within the DNAPL source zone to evaluate the feasibility and design parameters for the full-scale SEE system specified in the ROD. The ROD calls for SEE as the primary technology for DNAPL mass removal within the identified source zone, supplemented by soil excavation and thermal desorption.

**Pilot Test 1** was conducted in the vicinity of boring PDI-SB-06 within the central DNAPL zone. The test utilized a single injection well screened from 8 to 18 feet bgs and a single extraction well located 15 feet from the injection point, screened at the same interval. Steam was injected at approximately 250°F and 15 pounds per square inch (psi) for a period of 14 consecutive days. Four temperature monitoring points were installed at radial distances of 5, 10, 15, and 20 feet from the injection well to track thermal propagation. Temperature data indicated that the effective steam distribution radius --- defined as the radius at which subsurface temperatures reached at least 200°F --- was approximately 12 to 15 feet from the injection well. The 15-foot monitoring point achieved target temperature on Day 10, while the 20-foot monitoring point did not reach target temperature during the test period. VOC mass recovery during Pilot Test 1 was estimated at approximately 85% of the targeted VOC mass within the test cell area, based on pre- and post-test soil sampling and extracted vapor/condensate analysis.

**Pilot Test 2** was conducted in the vicinity of boring PDI-SB-10 in the eastern portion of the DNAPL zone, where subsurface lithology includes a more prominent silt lens between 10 and 14 feet bgs. The same injection/extraction well configuration and operating parameters were employed. Temperature monitoring at this location indicated an effective steam distribution radius of approximately 10 to 12 feet, reflecting the reduced permeability associated with the silt-rich zone. The 15-foot monitoring point did not consistently achieve target temperature during the 14-day test period. VOC mass recovery during Pilot Test 2 was estimated at approximately 72% of the targeted VOC mass within the test cell area.

The difference in performance between the two pilot tests reflects the influence of lithologic heterogeneity on steam propagation. The siltier conditions encountered in the Pilot Test 2 area reduced the effective treatment radius and mass recovery efficiency, indicating that the full-scale SEE system design must account for variable subsurface conditions across the 2.8-acre DNAPL zone.

Based on the pilot test results, we recommend fourteen (14) injection/extraction well pairs to achieve adequate coverage of the 2.8-acre DNAPL source zone, consistent with the ROD specification. This well count is predicated on an assumed effective treatment radius of 12 feet, which represents the lower bound of the range observed in Pilot Test 1 and the upper bound of the range observed in Pilot Test 2. At a 12-foot effective radius, 14 well pairs provide overlapping treatment coverage across the source area with an appropriate factor of safety.

However, if subsequent full-scale pilot testing confirms that steam distribution radii consistently achieve the upper range observed in Pilot Test 1 (i.e., 15-foot radius), it may be feasible to achieve adequate coverage with as few as 12 well pairs, provided that well placement is optimized based on site-specific lithologic data and that real-time temperature monitoring confirms adequate steam distribution during operations. We note that the ROD specified 14 well pairs and that departures from the ROD-specified well count should be supported by demonstrated performance data from full-scale operations. No full-scale pilot testing has been conducted to date, and the conditional reduction to 12 well pairs should not be adopted in the RAWP without such data.

The complete pilot test data, including temperature monitoring logs, injection/extraction rate records, and mass recovery calculations, are provided in Attachment C.

**[3.4 Estimated Excavation Volume Refinement --- OU-1]{.underline}**

Based on the PDI results, Terraverde re-estimated the soil excavation volume for OU-1 using the updated lateral and vertical extent data from the twelve PDI borings. Excavation volume estimates were developed using three-dimensional interpolation of contamination extent between boring locations, applying the industrial PRGs as the basis for defining the excavation limits.

Using the ROD-specified excavation depth of 15 feet bgs applied across OU-1, the updated volume estimate is approximately 40,500 cubic yards. This represents a modest reduction from the ROD\'s estimated volume of 42,000 cubic yards. The reduction is attributed to refined lateral extent data from the PDI borings, which indicate that the western margin of the contamination plume does not extend as far as estimated in the RI. The vertical extent data, however, support the ROD\'s assumed 15-foot depth in the central and eastern areas.

If a reduced excavation depth of 12 feet bgs were adopted in areas where PDI data supports shallower contamination --- specifically, the areas corresponding to the seven borings showing contamination above 12 feet --- while maintaining a 15-foot depth in the five deep-contamination boring areas, the estimated volume would decrease to approximately 38,200 cubic yards. This blended approach is presented for informational purposes; recommendations regarding excavation depth are addressed in Section 5.1.

For reference, a uniform 12-foot excavation depth applied across all of OU-1, without differentiation between shallow and deep contamination areas, would yield a similar volume estimate but would leave contaminated soil in place in the central and eastern areas where COC concentrations exceed PRGs below 12 feet bgs.

**[4. OU-2 PDI Results --- Wastewater Lagoon Area]{.underline}**

**[4.1 Contamination Extent and Native Clay Delineation]{.underline}**

The nine OU-2 soil borings (PDI-LG-01 through PDI-LG-09) were distributed across the three former unlined lagoon areas to characterize the vertical and lateral extent of residual contamination and to delineate the native clay confining layer that forms the base of the contaminated zone. The complete analytical results are provided in Attachment A.

PCP contamination was detected in all nine borings at concentrations exceeding the residential PRG of 0.3 mg/kg. Seven of nine borings (PDI-LG-01, -02, -03, -05, -06, -07, and -09) exhibited PCP concentrations exceeding the industrial PRG of 3.8 mg/kg within the upper 10 feet of the soil column, with maximum concentrations ranging from 5.2 mg/kg to 34 mg/kg. The two borings that did not exceed the industrial PCP PRG (PDI-LG-04 and PDI-LG-08) are located at the northern margin of Lagoon 1 and the eastern margin of Lagoon 3, respectively, and exhibited PCP concentrations of 2.1 and 3.4 mg/kg, respectively, just below the industrial PRG.

Hexavalent chromium was detected above the industrial PRG of 6.3 mg/kg in six of nine borings within the upper 8 feet of the soil profile. Concentrations ranged from 8.2 mg/kg (PDI-LG-04) to 78 mg/kg (PDI-LG-06, at 4 feet bgs within the Lagoon 2 footprint). Benzo(a)pyrene was detected at concentrations above the industrial PRG of 2.1 mg/kg in three of nine borings, with concentrations ranging from 2.8 to 6.4 mg/kg.

A critical objective of the OU-2 PDI was the delineation of the native clay confining layer. The ROD requires excavation \"to the native clay layer,\" which was estimated at approximately 12 feet bgs based on RI-phase data. The PDI borings encountered the native clay layer at the following depths:

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Boring ID**           **Depth to Native Clay (ft bgs)**   **Lagoon Area**
  ----------------------- ----------------------------------- -----------------------
  PDI-LG-01               11.5                                Lagoon 1

  PDI-LG-02               12.0                                Lagoon 1

  PDI-LG-03               12.5                                Lagoon 1

  PDI-LG-04               11.8                                Lagoon 2

  PDI-LG-05               13.0                                Lagoon 3

  PDI-LG-06               12.2                                Lagoon 2

  PDI-LG-07               11.5                                Lagoon 2

  PDI-LG-08               12.8                                Lagoon 3

  PDI-LG-09               12.0                                Lagoon 3
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The native clay layer was encountered at depths ranging from 11.5 to 13.0 feet bgs across the lagoon area, with an average depth of approximately 12.1 feet bgs. The greatest clay depths were observed in the Lagoon 3 area (PDI-LG-05 at 13.0 feet and PDI-LG-08 at 12.8 feet), while the shallowest clay contacts were encountered at the margins of Lagoons 1 and 2 (PDI-LG-01 and PDI-LG-07, both at 11.5 feet).

Native clay was encountered between 11.5 and 13.0 feet bgs across the lagoon area. To ensure excavation to the native clay layer in all areas, as required by the ROD, excavation depths will need to extend to at least 13 feet bgs in portions of the lagoon footprint, particularly in the vicinity of Lagoon 3 (PDI-LG-05 and PDI-LG-08).

Contamination was detected at or just above the clay contact in four of nine borings (PDI-LG-03, PDI-LG-05, PDI-LG-06, and PDI-LG-08), confirming that contaminated soils extend to the clay surface and that excavation to the clay layer is necessary to achieve removal of the contaminated materials. In PDI-LG-05, PCP was detected at 7.8 mg/kg at a depth of 12.5 feet bgs, just 0.5 feet above the clay contact at 13.0 feet. No contamination was detected within the native clay layer itself, confirming the clay\'s effectiveness as a natural confining unit.

**[4.2 Geotechnical Evaluation --- Containment Cell Foundation]{.underline}**

Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants, LLC conducted a geotechnical evaluation of the native clay layer and surrounding soils within the OU-2 footprint to support the design of the containment cell specified in the ROD. Pinnacle\'s investigation included collection and laboratory testing of undisturbed Shelby tube samples from the native clay layer at four boring locations, grain size analyses, Atterberg limits testing, unconfined compressive strength testing, and consolidation testing. The full Pinnacle geotechnical report is provided as Attachment B.

Key geotechnical findings are summarized as follows. The native clay layer exhibits a permeability of approximately 1 × 10⁻⁷ cm/sec, classifying it as a low-permeability formation suitable as a natural foundation layer for the containment cell. The clay is classified as CL (lean clay) to CH (fat clay) under the Unified Soil Classification System, with plasticity indices ranging from 22 to 38. The bearing capacity of the subgrade soils underlying the proposed containment cell footprint was determined to be adequate for the anticipated loading conditions, including the weight of the compacted contaminated soils, cover system, and the liner system components.

The ROD specifies a composite liner system for the containment cell consisting of a 60-mil high-density polyethylene (HDPE) geomembrane over a minimum 2-foot (24-inch) compacted clay liner. This specification is consistent with RCRA Subtitle C requirements per 40 CFR 264.310 for hazardous waste containment.

Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants recommends a minimum 60-mil HDPE liner over 24 inches of compacted clay to satisfy the RCRA-equivalent performance standard specified in the ROD. Pinnacle noted that the available on-site clay materials, when properly excavated, processed, and compacted to at least 95% of standard Proctor maximum dry density at a moisture content within 2% of optimum, can achieve the requisite 1 × 10⁻⁷ cm/sec permeability for the compacted clay component. Pinnacle further noted that the use of on-site clay materials for the compacted clay liner layer would be technically feasible and cost-effective, provided that appropriate construction quality assurance (CQA) procedures are implemented during placement and compaction. Pinnacle did not recommend or evaluate any alternative liner configurations that would reduce the thickness of either the HDPE geomembrane or the compacted clay component below the ROD specification.

**[4.3 Estimated Excavation Volume Refinement --- OU-2]{.underline}**

Based on the PDI data showing the native clay layer at depths between 11.5 and 13.0 feet bgs, Terraverde re-estimated the OU-2 excavation volume using the variable clay contact depth as the base of excavation, consistent with the ROD requirement to excavate \"to the native clay layer.\"

Assuming excavation to the native clay layer at each location (variable depth, 11.5 to 13.0 feet bgs), the updated volume estimate is approximately 27,800 cubic yards. This represents a modest reduction from the ROD\'s estimated volume of 28,500 cubic yards, attributable to minor refinements in the lateral extent of the lagoon footprint based on PDI boring data and updated topographic survey information.

If a uniform excavation depth of 10 feet bgs were assumed across the OU-2 footprint, the estimated volume would be approximately 24,100 cubic yards. However, this approach would not reach the native clay layer in any of the PDI boring locations --- the shallowest clay contact was encountered at 11.5 feet bgs --- and would leave between 1.5 and 3.0 feet of contaminated material in place above the clay surface across the lagoon area. A 10-foot uniform excavation depth is therefore not recommended and is presented here solely for comparative purposes.

**[5. Preliminary Recommendations]{.underline}**

**[5.1 OU-1 Recommendations]{.underline}**

**Excavation Depth.** Based on the PDI results, we recommend maintaining the ROD-specified excavation depth of 15 feet bgs as the design basis across OU-1. While 7 of 12 borings indicate contamination may be limited to the upper 12 feet, 5 of 12 borings --- concentrated in the central and eastern portions of the site --- show contamination at or below 15 feet. A blanket reduction of the excavation depth to 12 feet would leave contaminated soils in place in approximately 42% of the investigated area, including areas where COC concentrations substantially exceed industrial PRGs. The borings exhibiting deep contamination are spatially coincident with the DNAPL source zone, where contaminant concentrations are highest and the environmental risk is greatest.

We recommend that the RAWP incorporate a variable excavation depth approach, with 15 feet bgs as the default excavation depth and confirmation sampling protocols to verify clean conditions before reducing depth in specific areas. Under this approach, the excavation depth could be reduced to 12 feet bgs in areas where confirmation samples collected at the 12-foot horizon demonstrate COC concentrations below industrial PRGs. This approach preserves the protectiveness of the ROD remedy while allowing for site-specific optimization where supported by data.

**Steam-Enhanced Extraction Well Pairs.** We recommend fourteen (14) injection/extraction well pairs, consistent with the ROD, as the design basis for the full-scale SEE system. The pilot test data support 14 well pairs as the minimum number necessary to achieve adequate thermal coverage of the 2.8-acre DNAPL source zone, accounting for the variable steam distribution radii observed in the two pilot tests (10 to 15 feet). A reduction to 12 well pairs may be feasible but should be contingent on full-scale pilot testing demonstrating that steam distribution radii consistently achieve the 15-foot effective radius observed in Pilot Test 1 under the range of lithologic conditions present across the source zone. We do not recommend adopting 12 well pairs in the RAWP absent such data. Full-scale pilot testing, if pursued, should be conducted as a discrete phase of work prior to finalizing the SEE system design.

**Thermal Desorption Treatment Standard.** The PDI did not generate data bearing on the thermal desorption treatment standard. The ROD specifies a treatment standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs for thermally treated soils prior to on-site reuse or off-site disposal. The RAWP should incorporate the ROD-specified standard of 1 mg/kg total VOCs. Any proposed deviation from this standard would require EPA approval through a formal modification process.

**[5.2 OU-2 Recommendations]{.underline}**

**Excavation Depth.** We recommend that excavation at OU-2 proceed to the native clay layer, as specified in the ROD. The PDI demonstrates that the clay layer ranges from 11.5 to 13.0 feet bgs, and excavation should be carried to the clay contact in all areas. A uniform 10-foot excavation depth would be insufficient to reach the native clay in any of the PDI boring locations and would leave contaminated material in place above the clay layer across the entire lagoon footprint. The RAWP should specify excavation to the clay contact as the performance standard, with field verification of the clay surface during construction to guide real-time excavation depth adjustments. In areas such as the Lagoon 3 footprint where the clay layer occurs at 13.0 feet bgs, excavation will need to extend to that depth.

**Containment Cell Liner.** The containment cell liner system should conform to the ROD specification of a 60-mil HDPE geomembrane over 24 inches of compacted clay, consistent with Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants\' recommendation and RCRA Subtitle C requirements. The PDI geotechnical evaluation confirmed that on-site native clay materials are suitable for the compacted clay component when properly processed and compacted. There is no technical basis in the PDI data for reducing the liner system below the ROD specification. The RAWP should incorporate the ROD-specified liner system with appropriate construction quality assurance provisions.

**Monitoring.** The ROD requires installation of a minimum of eight (8) downgradient monitoring wells as part of the long-term groundwater monitoring program for OU-2. We recommend that the RAWP incorporate this requirement and that well locations be finalized during remedial design based on updated groundwater flow modeling using the PDI permeability data.

**[6. Limitations and Next Steps]{.underline}**

The results and conclusions presented in this memorandum are based on the data generated from the PDI field investigation, including the specific number and locations of soil borings, well points, and pilot test installations described herein. Subsurface conditions between and beyond boring locations may differ from those observed at the investigated points. The PDI data represent a refinement of the RI-phase characterization but may not capture all subsurface variability across the 62-acre site. Additional data collection may be warranted during remedial design or construction to address localized conditions not fully characterized by the PDI.

We recommend that the RAWP incorporate adaptive management provisions to address variability in contamination depth at OU-1 and clay layer depth at OU-2. Such provisions should include confirmation sampling protocols, real-time field screening during excavation, and decision frameworks for adjusting excavation depths based on field conditions encountered during construction.

As noted in Section 3.3, additional pilot testing for the SEE system is recommended before finalizing the injection/extraction well pair count in the RAWP. This testing would provide the performance data necessary to evaluate whether a reduction from 14 to 12 well pairs is technically supportable.

A draft RAWP is targeted for completion by December 2024 for internal review by CCH and its legal counsel prior to formal submission to EPA Region 5. The formal RAWP submission is targeted for January 2025. Upon submission, the EPA 60-day review period will commence in accordance with the Consent Decree schedule and Statement of Work.

Terraverde is available to discuss the PDI results with CCH, Whitmore & Associates LLP, and EPA/Ohio EPA project staff as needed to support the transition from the PDI phase to remedial design. Please do not hesitate to contact the undersigned to schedule a meeting or request additional information.

**[7. Attachments]{.underline}**

The following attachments are referenced in this memorandum. These documents are provided under separate cover and are incorporated herein by reference.

**Attachment A:** PDI Boring Logs and Analytical Results Summary Tables (OU-1: PDI-SB-01 through PDI-SB-12; OU-2: PDI-LG-01 through PDI-LG-09)

**Attachment B:** Pinnacle Geotechnical Consultants, LLC --- Geotechnical Investigation Report, OU-2 Containment Cell Foundation Evaluation (dated September 2024)

**Attachment C:** SEE Pilot Test Data Sheets and Temperature Monitoring Results

**Attachment D:** PDI Boring Location Map (Figure 1: OU-1 Boring Locations; Figure 2: OU-2 Boring Locations)

**Attachment E:** Clearwater Analytical Laboratories, Inc. --- Laboratory Data Packages and Data Validation Reports

Respectfully submitted,

import re
from docx import Document
from docx.shared import Pt, Inches, RGBColor
from docx.enum.text import WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH
from docx.enum.table import WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT
from docx.oxml.ns import qn
from docx.oxml import OxmlElement

doc = Document()
sec = doc.sections[0]
sec.left_margin = sec.right_margin = Inches(1)
sec.top_margin = sec.bottom_margin = Inches(1)
st = doc.styles["Normal"]
st.font.name = "Calibri"; st.font.size = Pt(11)
st.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "Calibri")
for lvl, sz in ((1, 14), (2, 12), (3, 11)):
    h = doc.styles["Heading %d" % lvl]
    h.font.name = "Calibri"; h.font.size = Pt(sz); h.font.bold = True
    h.font.color.rgb = RGBColor(0x1F, 0x3A, 0x5F)
    h.element.rPr.rFonts.set(qn("w:eastAsia"), "Calibri")

def runs(p, text, size=None):
    parts = re.split(r"(\*\*.+?\*\*|__.+?__)", text)
    for part in parts:
        if not part: continue
        if part.startswith("**"):
            r = p.add_run(part[2:-2]); r.bold = True
        elif part.startswith("__"):
            r = p.add_run(part[2:-2]); r.italic = True
        else:
            r = p.add_run(part)
        if size: r.font.size = Pt(size)
    return p

def H(text, lvl=1):
    return doc.add_heading(text, level=lvl)

def P(text, size=None, align=None, space=6):
    p = doc.add_paragraph()
    runs(p, text, size)
    p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(space)
    if align == "c": p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.CENTER
    return p

def B(text, lvl=0):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style="List Bullet" if lvl == 0 else "List Bullet 2")
    runs(p, text); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
    return p

def N(text):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style="List Number")
    runs(p, text); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
    return p

def shade(cell, hexcolor):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement("w:shd")
    shd.set(qn("w:val"), "clear"); shd.set(qn("w:color"), "auto"); shd.set(qn("w:fill"), hexcolor)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def T(header, rows, widths, size=8.5, sevcol=None):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(header))
    t.style = "Table Grid"; t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    t.autofit = False
    for i, h in enumerate(header):
        c = t.rows[0].cells[i]; c.text = ""
        runs(c.paragraphs[0], "**" + h + "**", size); shade(c, "D9E2F3")
    for row in rows:
        cells = t.add_row().cells
        for i, v in enumerate(row):
            cells[i].text = ""
            lines = str(v).split("\n")
            runs(cells[i].paragraphs[0], lines[0], size)
            for ln in lines[1:]:
                runs(cells[i].add_paragraph(), ln, size)
            if sevcol is not None and i == sevcol:
                s = str(v).lower()
                if s.startswith("critical"): shade(cells[i], "F4CCCC")
                elif s.startswith("high"): shade(cells[i], "FCE5CD")
                elif s.startswith("moderate"): shade(cells[i], "FFF2CC")
                elif s.startswith("low") or s.startswith("consistent"): shade(cells[i], "D9EAD3")
    for row in t.rows:
        for i, w in enumerate(widths):
            row.cells[i].width = Inches(w)
    # repeat header
    trPr = t.rows[0]._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    el = OxmlElement("w:tblHeader"); el.set(qn("w:val"), "true"); trPr.append(el)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return t

    runs(p, text); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3)
    return p

def shade(cell, hexcolor):
    tcPr = cell._tc.get_or_add_tcPr()
    shd = OxmlElement("w:shd")
    shd.set(qn("w:val"), "clear"); shd.set(qn("w:color"), "auto"); shd.set(qn("w:fill"), hexcolor)
    tcPr.append(shd)

def T(header, rows, widths, size=8.5, sevcol=None):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(header))
    t.style = "Table Grid"; t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    t.autofit = False
    for i, h in enumerate(header):
        c = t.rows[0].cells[i]; c.text = ""
        runs(c.paragraphs[0], "**" + h + "**", size); shade(c, "D9E2F3")
    for row in rows:
        cells = t.add_row().cells
        for i, v in enumerate(row):
            cells[i].text = ""
            lines = str(v).split("\n")
            runs(cells[i].paragraphs[0], lines[0], size)
            for ln in lines[1:]:
                runs(cells[i].add_paragraph(), ln, size)
            if sevcol is not None and i == sevcol:
                s = str(v).lower()
                if s.startswith("critical"): shade(cells[i], "F4CCCC")
                elif s.startswith("high"): shade(cells[i], "FCE5CD")
                elif s.startswith("moderate"): shade(cells[i], "FFF2CC")
                elif s.startswith("low") or s.startswith("consistent"): shade(cells[i], "D9EAD3")
    for row in t.rows:
        for i, w in enumerate(widths):
            row.cells[i].width = Inches(w)
    # repeat header
    trPr = t.rows[0]._tr.get_or_add_trPr()
    el = OxmlElement("w:tblHeader"); el.set(qn("w:val"), "true"); trPr.append(el)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return t
EOF

B("**Community-facing departures that directly match the CAG’s complaints:** the VOC fenceline action level is doubled (5 → 10 ppmv); the haul route moves from State Route 47 to County Road 12, which the CAG says runs through Millhaven Heights past a daycare and an elementary school; and OU-4 ecological monitoring is cut from 5 to 3 years, with ODNR left out of the Habitat Restoration Plan approval.")
B("**A credibility problem that compounds all of the above.** The RAWP repeatedly says the reductions are “optimized” or “refined” based on the 2024 PDI. B("**The cost estimate tracks the scope cuts.** The RAWP estimate is $72.1 million against the ROD’s $89.4 million, a drop of $17.3 million (19.4%). P("**Recommendation.** CCH should not defend the RAWP as submitted. We recommend that CCH promptly withdraw it, or tell EPA it will revise it, and resubmit a version that conforms to the ROD. Any optimization CCH still wants should be pursued separately through a properly documented CD ¶35 modification request. The PDI memo shows one such optimization is supportable: variable-depth excavation at OU-1 governed by confirmation sampling. Under CD ¶¶49–52, stipulated-penalty exposure for Major Deviations generally runs from the date a deficient component becomes operational (¶50). If the RAWP is corrected before construction, most of that exposure can be avoided. Exposure that may already exist (late submittal, missing certification, incomplete ARAR matrix, haul-route and plan deficiencies) is discussed in Part VIII.")

H("II. Documents Reviewed and Assumptions", 1)
T(["Document", "Date / Author", "Role in this analysis"], [
 ["Record of Decision (ROD)", "Sept. 15, 2021; EPA Region 5 (Volkov; Kendrick, Acting RA); Ohio EPA concurrence Sept. 10, 2021", "Controlling statement of the selected remedy, RAOs, cleanup levels, design minimums, and 47 ARARs (Table 2-1)"],
 ["Consent Decree (CD)", "Case No. 3:20-cv-00487-JHR (N.D.  ["Remedial Action Work Plan (RAWP)", "Dec. 20, 2024 (certified by K. Brannick, P.E.); submitted Jan. 15, 2025; Terraverde Project No. TVE-2024-0347", "Document under review"],
 ["PDI Summary Memorandum", "Oct. 15, 2024; Brannick to Yamashita, cc Eng; marked privileged; Project No. TVE-2024-0387", "Underlying design data and Terraverde’s own recommendations for OU-1 and OU-2"],
 ["CAG letter to EPA", "Feb. 5, 2025; Ellen Dorsey to Dr. Volkov, cc R. Hess", "Community concerns likely to shape EPA’s review and any public process"],
], [1.6, 2.2, 2.7], size=8.5)
P("**Assumptions.** (1) We have not been given any EPA comments, approval, disapproval, ESD, or ROD Amendment issued after the RAWP was submitted.
